entries.b886c310ed69ea54481f9db7d8e1bcf95990f507: <div sID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Isa.16" sID="Isa.16"/> <div eID="gen15833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15834" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15835" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes the burden of Moab. In it, I. The prophet gives good counsel to the Moabites, to reform what was amiss among them, and particularly to be kind to God's people, as the likeliest way to prevent the judgments before threatened, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. Fearing they would not take this counsel (they were so proud), he goes on to foretel the lamentable devastation of their country, and the confusion they should be brought to, and this within three years, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6-Isa.16.14">ver. 6-14</reference>.
entries.7ceaaf8c53ea738f94571b452681ba721ec4e3f1: <div eID="gen15835" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15834" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortations to Moab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen15836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Send ye the lamb to the ruler of the land from Sela to the wilderness, unto the mount of the daughter of Zion. <hi type="super">2</hi> For it shall be, <hi type="italic">that,</hi> as a wandering bird cast out of the nest, <hi type="italic">so</hi> the daughters of Moab shall be at the fords of Arnon. <hi type="super">3</hi> Take counsel, execute judgment; make thy shadow as the night in the midst of the noonday; hide the outcasts; bewray not him that wandereth. <hi type="super">4</hi> Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a covert to them from the face of the spoiler: for the extortioner is at an end, the spoiler ceaseth, the oppressors are consumed out of the land. <hi type="super">5</hi> And in mercy shall the throne be established: and he shall sit upon it in truth in the tabernacle of David, judging, and seeking judgment, and hasting righteousness. <div eID="gen15836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15837" type="x-p"/> God has made it to appear that he delights not in the ruin of sinners by telling them what they may do to prevent the ruin; so he does here to Moab. <div eID="gen15837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15838" type="x-p"/> I. He advises them to be just to the house of David, and to pay the tribute they had formerly covenanted to pay to the kings of his line (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Send you the lamb to the ruler of the land.</hi> David made the Moabites tributaries to him, <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2 Sam. viii. 2</reference>. They <hi type="italic">became his servants, and brought gifts.</hi> Afterwards they paid their tribute to the kings of Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2 Kings iii. 4</reference>), and paid it in lambs. Now the prophet requires them to pay it to Hezekiah. Let it be raised and levied from all parts of the country, <hi type="italic">from Selah,</hi> a frontier city of Moab on the one side, <hi type="italic">to the wilderness,</hi> a boundary of the kingdom on the other side: and let it be sent, where it should be sent, <hi type="italic">to the mount of the daughter of Zion,</hi> the city of David. Some take it as an advice to send a lamb for a sacrifice to God, <hi type="italic">the ruler of the earth</hi> (so it may be read), the Lord of the whole earth, ruler of all lands, the land of Moab as well as the land of Israel, "Send it to the temple built on Mount Zion." And some think it is in this sense spoken ironically, upbraiding the Moabites with their folly in delaying to repent and make their peace with God. "Now you would be glad to send a lamb to Mount Zion, to make the God of Israel your friend; but it is too late: the decree has gone forth, the consumption is determined, and the <hi type="italic">daughters of Moab</hi> shall be cast out <hi type="italic">as a wandering bird,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">v. 2</reference>. I rather take it as good advice seriously given, like that of Daniel to Nebuchadnezzar when he was reading him his doom, <reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Dan. iv. 27</reference>. <hi type="italic">Break off thy sins by righteousness, if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.</hi> And it is applicable to the great gospel duty of submission to Christ, as the ruler of the land, and our ruler: "Send him the lamb, the best you have, yourselves a living sacrifice. When you come to God, the great ruler, come in the name of the Lamb, the Lamb of God. <hi type="italic">For else it shall be</hi>" (so we may read it) "<hi type="italic">that, as a wandering bird cast out of the nest, so shall the daughters of Moab be.</hi> If you will not pay your quit-rent, your just tribute to the king of Judah, you shall be turned out of your houses: <hi type="italic">The daughters of Moab</hi> (the country villages, or the women of your country) shall flutter about the <hi type="italic">fords of Arnon,</hi> attempting that way to make their escape to some other land, <hi type="italic">like a wandering bird thrown out of the nest</hi> half-fledged." Those that will not submit to Christ, nor be gathered under the shadow of his wings, shall be <hi type="italic">as a bird that wanders from her nest,</hi> that shall either be snatched up by the next bird of prey or shall wander endlessly in continual frights. Those that will not yield to the fear of God shall be made to yield to the fear of every thing else. <div eID="gen15838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15839" type="x-p"/> II. He advises them to be <hi type="italic">kind to the seed of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">v. 3</reference>): "Take counsel, call a convention, and consult among yourselves what is fit to be done in the present critical juncture; and you will find it your best way to execute judgment, to reverse all the unrighteous decrees you have made, by which you have put hardships upon the people of God, and, in token of your repentance for them, study now how to oblige them, and this shall be accepted of God more than all burnt-offering and sacrifice." <div eID="gen15839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15840" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet foresaw some storm coming upon the people of God, perhaps the good people of the ten tribes, or of the two and a half on the other side Jordan, whose country joined to that of Moab, and who, by the merciful providence of God, escaped the fury of the Assyrian army, had their lives given them for a prey, and were reserved for better times, but were put to the utmost extremity to shift for their own safety. The danger and trouble they were in were like the scorching heat at noon; the face of the spoiler was very fierce upon them and the oppressor and extortioner were ready to swallow them up after stripping them of what they had. <div eID="gen15840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15841" type="x-p"/> 2. He bespeaks a shelter for them in the land of Moab, when their own land was made too hot for them. This judgment they must execute; thus wisely must they do for themselves, and thus kindly must they deal with the people of God. If they would themselves continue in their habitations, let them now open their doors to the distressed dispersed members of God's church, and be to them like a cool shade to those that <hi type="italic">bear the burden and heat of the day.</hi> Let them not discover those that absconded among them, nor deliver them up to the pursuers that made search for them: "<hi type="italic">Betray not him that wandereth,</hi> nor deliver him up" (as the Edomites did, <reference osisRef="Obad.1.13-Obad.1.14">Obad. 13, 14</reference>), "but <hi type="italic">hide the outcasts.</hi>" This was that good work by which Rahab's faith was justified, and proved to be sincere, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.31">Heb. xi. 31</reference>. "Nay, do not only hide them for a time, but, if there be occasion, let them be naturalized: <hi type="italic">Let my outcasts dwell with thee, Moab</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">v. 4</reference>); find a lodging for them and <hi type="italic">be thou a covert to them.</hi> Let them be taken under the protection of the government, though they are but poor, and likely to be a charge to thee." Note, (1.) It is often the lot even of those who are Israelites indeed to be outcasts, driven out of house and harbour by persecution or war, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.37">Heb. xi. 37</reference>. (2.) God owns them when men reject and disown them. They are <hi type="italic">outcasts,</hi> but they are <hi type="italic">my outcasts.</hi> The Lord knows those that are his wherever he finds them, even where no one else knows them. (3.) God will find a rest and shelter for his outcasts; for, though they are persecuted, they are not forsaken. He will himself be their dwelling-place if they have no other, and in him they shall be at home. (4.) God can, when he pleases, raise up friends for his people even among Moabites, when they can find none in all the land of Israel that can and dare shelter them. The earth often helps the woman, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.16">Rev. xii. 16</reference>. (5.) Those that expect to find favour when they are in trouble themselves must show favour to those that are in trouble; and what service is done to God's outcasts shall no doubt be recompensed one way or other. <div eID="gen15841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15842" type="x-p"/> 3. He assures them of the mercy God had in store for his people. (1.) That they should not long need their kindness, or be troublesome to them: <hi type="italic">For the extortioner is almost at an end</hi> already, <hi type="italic">and the spoiler ceases.</hi> God's people shall not be long outcasts; they <hi type="italic">shall have tribulation ten days</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Rev. ii. 10</reference>), and that is all. The spoiler would never cease spoiling if he might have his will; but God has him in a chain. <hi type="italic">Hitherto he shall go, but no further.</hi> (2.) That they should, ere long, be in a capacity to return their kindness (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">v. 5</reference>): "Though the throne of the ten tribes be sunk and overturned, yet <hi type="italic">the throne of David shall be established in mercy,</hi> by the mercy they receive from God and the mercy they show to others; and by the same methods may your throne be established if you please." It would engage great men to be kind to the people of God if they would but observe, as they easily might, how often such conduct brings the blessing of God upon kingdoms and families. "Make Hezekiah your friend, for you will find it your interest to do so upon the account both of the grace of God in him and the presence of God with him. He <hi type="italic">shall sit upon the throne in truth,</hi> and then he does indeed sit in honour and sit firmly. Then he shall sit <hi type="italic">judging,</hi> and will then be a protector to those that have been a shelter to the people of God." And see in him the character of a good magistrate. [1.] He shall <hi type="italic">seek judgment;</hi> that is, he shall seek occasions of doing right to those that are wronged, and shall punish the injurious even before they are complained of: or he shall diligently search into every cause brought before him, that he may find where the right lies. [2.] He shall <hi type="italic">hasten righteousness,</hi> and not delay to do justice, nor keep those long waiting that make application to him for the redress of their grievances. Though he seeks judgment, and deliberates upon it, yet he does not, under pretence of deliberation, stay the progress of the streams of justice. Let the Moabites take example by this, and then assure themselves that their state shall be established.
entries.54c3f71a383c773cd0f135fa24826fd94e3f0907: <div eID="gen15842" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pride of Moab; The Threatening against Moab; The Doom of Moab. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 725.)</title> <div sID="gen15843" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> We have heard of the pride of Moab; <hi type="italic">he is</hi> very proud: <hi type="italic">even</hi> of his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath: <hi type="italic">but</hi> his lies <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> so. <hi type="super">7</hi> Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab, every one shall howl: for the foundations of Kir-hareseth shall ye mourn; surely <hi type="italic">they are</hi> stricken. <hi type="super">8</hi> For the fields of Heshbon languish, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the vine of Sibmah: the lords of the heathen have broken down the principal plants thereof, they are come <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Jazer, they wandered <hi type="italic">through</hi> the wilderness: her branches are stretched out, they are gone over the sea. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore I will bewail with the weeping of Jazer the vine of Sibmah: I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon, and Elealeh: for the shouting for thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen. <hi type="super">10</hi> And gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field; and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shouting: the treaders shall tread out no wine in <hi type="italic">their</hi> presses; I have made <hi type="italic">their vintage</hi> shouting to cease. <hi type="super">11</hi> Wherefore my bowels shall sound like a harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kir-haresh. <hi type="super">12</hi> And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary on the high place, that he shall come to his sanctuary to pray; but he shall not prevail. <hi type="super">13</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the word that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken concerning Moab since that time. <hi type="super">14</hi> But now the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath spoken, saying, Within three years, as the years of a hireling, and the glory of Moab shall be contemned, with all that great multitude; and the remnant <hi type="italic">shall be</hi> very small <hi type="italic">and</hi> feeble. <div eID="gen15843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15844" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The sins with which Moab is charged, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">v. 6</reference>. The prophet seems to check himself for going about to give good counsel to the Moabites, concluding they would not take the advice he gave them. He told them their duty (whether they would hear or whether they would forbear), but despairs of working any good upon them; he would have healed them, but they would not be healed. Those that will not be counselled cannot be helped. Their sins were, 1. Pride. This is most insisted upon; for perhaps there are more precious souls ruined by pride than by any one lust whatsoever. The Moabites were notorious for this: "<hi type="italic">We have heard</hi> in both ears <hi type="italic">of the pride of Moab;</hi> it is what all their neighbours cry out shame upon them for. <hi type="italic">He is very proud;</hi> the body of the nation is so, forgetting the baseness of their origin and the brand of infamy fastened upon them by that law of God which forbade a Moabite to <hi type="italic">enter into the congregation of the Lord for ever,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.23.3">Deut. xxiii. 3</reference>. We have heard of <hi type="italic">his haughtiness and his pride.</hi> It is not the rash and rigid censure of one of two concerning them, but it is the character which all that know them will give of them. They are a proud people, and therefore they will not take good counsel when it is given them. They think themselves too wise to be advised; therefore they will not take example by Hezekiah to do justly and love mercy. They scorn to make him their pattern, for they think themselves able to teach him. They are proud, and therefore will not be subject to God himself nor regard the warnings he gives them. <hi type="italic">The wicked, in the pride of his countenance, will not seek after God.</hi> They are proud, and therefore will not entertain and protect God's outcasts; they scorn to have any thing to do with them." But this is not all:—2. "We have heard of <hi type="italic">his wrath</hi> too (for those that are very proud are commonly very passionate), particularly his wrath against the people of God, whom therefore he will rather persecute than protect. 3. It is with <hi type="italic">his lies</hi> that he gains the gratifications of his pride and his passion; <hi type="italic">but his lies shall not be so;</hi> he shall not compass his proud and angry projects as he hoped he should." Some read it, <hi type="italic">His haughtiness, his pride, and his wrath, are greater than his strength.</hi> "We know that, if we lay at his mercy, we should find no mercy with him, but he has not power equal to his malice. His pride draws down ruin upon him; for it is the preface to destruction, and he has not strength to ward it off." <div eID="gen15844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15845" type="x-p"/> II. The sorrows with which Moab is threatened (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab.</hi> All the inhabitants shall bitterly lament the ruin of their country. They shall complain one to another: <hi type="italic">Every one shall howl</hi> in despair, and not one shall either see any cause or have any heart to encourage his friend. Observe, <div eID="gen15845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15846" type="x-p"/> 1. The causes of this sorrow. (1.) The destruction of their cities: <hi type="italic">For the foundations of Kir-haraseth shall you mourn.</hi> That great and strong city, which had held out against a mighty force (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.25">2 Kings iii. 25</reference>), should now be levelled with the ground, either burnt or broken down, and its foundations <hi type="italic">stricken,</hi> bruised and broken (so the word signifies); they shall howl when they see their splendid cities turned into ruinous heaps. (2.) The desolation of their country. Moab was famous for its fields and vineyards; but those shall all be laid waste by the invading army, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">v. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">10</reference>. See, [1.] What a fruitful pleasant country they had, as the garden of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Gen. xiii. 10</reference>. It was planted with choice and noble vines, with <hi type="italic">principal plants,</hi> which reached <hi type="italic">even to Jazer,</hi> a city in the tribe of Gad. The luxuriant branches of their vines <hi type="italic">wandered,</hi> and wound themselves along the ranges on which they were spread, even <hi type="italic">through the wilderness</hi> of Moab. There were vineyards there. Nay, they were <hi type="italic">stretched out,</hi> and went even to <hi type="italic">the sea,</hi> the Dead Sea: the best grapes grew in their hedge-rows. [2.] How merry and pleasant they had been in it. Many a time they had shouted <hi type="italic">for their summer fruits, and for their harvest,</hi> as the country people sometimes do with us when they have cut down all their corn. They had had <hi type="italic">joy and gladness</hi> in their fields and vineyards, <hi type="italic">singing</hi> and <hi type="italic">shouting at the treading of their grapes.</hi> Nothing is said of their praising God for their abundance, and giving him the glory of it. If they had made it the matter of their thanksgiving, they might still have had it the food and fuel of their lusts; see therefore, [3.] How they should be stripped of all. "The fields shall <hi type="italic">languish,</hi> all the fruits of them being carried away or trodden down; they cannot now enrich their owners as they have done, and therefore they languish. The soldiers, called here <hi type="italic">the lords of the heathen,</hi> shall break down all the plants, though they were <hi type="italic">principal plants,</hi> the choicest that could be got. Now the shouting for the enjoyment of the summer fruits has fallen, and is turned into howling for the loss of them. The joy of harvest has ceased; there is no more singing, no more shouting, for the treading out of wine. They have not what they have had to rejoice in, nor have they a disposition to rejoice; the ruin of their country has marred their mirth." Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> God can easily change the note of those that are most addicted to mirth and pleasure, can soon turn their laughter into mourning and their joy into heaviness. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Joy in God is, upon this account, far better than the joy of harvest, that it is what we cannot be robbed of, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.6-Ps.4.7">Ps. iv. 6, 7</reference>. Destroy the vines and the fig-trees, and you make all the mirth of a carnal heart to cease, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.11-Hos.2.12">Hos. ii. 11, 12</reference>. But a gracious soul can rejoice in the Lord as the God of its salvation even when the fig-tree does not blossom and there is no fruit in the vine, <reference osisRef="Hab.3.17-Hab.3.18">Hab. iii. 17, 18</reference>. In God therefore let us always rejoice with a holy triumph, and in other things let us always rejoice with a holy trembling, rejoice as though we rejoiced not. <div eID="gen15846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15847" type="x-p"/> 2. The concurrence of the prophet with them in this sorrow: "<hi type="italic">I will with weeping bewail Jazer, and the vine of Sibmah,</hi> and look with a compassionate concern upon the desolations of such a pleasant country. <hi type="italic">I will water thee with my tears, O Heshbon!</hi> and mingle them with thy tears;" nay (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">v. 11</reference>), it appears to be an inward grief: <hi type="italic">My bowels shall sound like a harp for Moab;</hi> it should make such an impression upon him that he should feel an inward trembling, like that of the strings of a harp when it is played upon. It well becomes God's prophets to acquaint themselves with grief; the great prophet did so. The afflictions of the world, as well as those of the church, should be afflictions to us. See <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">ch. xv. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen15847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15848" type="x-p"/> III. In the close of the chapter we have, 1. The insufficiency of the gods of Moab, the false gods, to help them, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.12">v. 12</reference>. "Moab shall be soon <hi type="italic">weary of the high place.</hi> He shall spend his spirits and strength in vain in praying to his idols; they cannot help him, and he shall be convinced that they cannot." It is seen that it is to no purpose to expect any relief from the high places on earth; it must come from above the hills. Men are generally so stupid that they will not believe, till they are made to see, the vanity of idols and of all creature-confidences, nor will come off from them till they are made weary of them. But, when he is weary of his high places, he will not go, as he should, to God's sanctuary, but to <hi type="italic">his</hi> sanctuary, to the temple of Chemosh, the principal idol of Moab (so it is generally understood); and he shall pray there to as little purpose, and as little to his own case and satisfaction, as he did in his high places; for, whatever honours idolaters give to their idols, they do not thereby make them at all the better able to help them. Whether they are the <hi type="italic">dii majorum gentium—gods of the higher order,</hi> or <hi type="italic">minorum—of the lower order,</hi> they are alike the creatures of men's fancy and the work of men's hands. Perhaps it may be meant of their coming to God's sanctuary. When they found they could have no succours from their own high places some of them would come to the temple of God at Jerusalem, to pray there, but in vain; he will justly send them back to <hi type="italic">the gods whom they have served,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.14">Judg. x. 14</reference>. 2. The sufficiency of the God of Israel, the only true God, to make good what he had spoken against them. (1.) The thing itself was long since determined (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">This is the word,</hi> this is the thing, <hi type="italic">that the Lord has spoken concerning Moab, since the time</hi> that he began to be so proud, and insolent, and abusive to God's people. The country was long ago doomed to ruin; this was enough to give an assurance of it that <hi type="italic">it is the word which the Lord has spoken;</hi> and, as he will never unsay what he has spoken, so all the power of hell and earth cannot gainsay it, or obstruct the execution of it. (2.) Now it was made known when it should be done. The time was before fixed in the counsel of God, but now it was revealed: <hi type="italic">The Lord has spoken</hi> that it shall be <hi type="italic">within three years,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">It is not for us to know,</hi> or covet to know, <hi type="italic">the times and the seasons,</hi> any further than God has thought fit to make them known, and so far we may and must take notice of them. See how God makes known his mind by degrees; the light of divine revelation shone more and more, and so does the light of divine grace in the heart. Observe, [1.] The sentence passed upon Moab: <hi type="italic">The glory of Moab shall be contemned,</hi> that is, it shall be contemptible, when all those things they have gloried in shall come to nothing. Such is the glory of this world, so fading and uncertain, admired awhile, but soon slighted. Let that therefore which will soon be contemptible in the eyes of others be always contemptible in our eyes in comparison with the <hi type="italic">far more exceeding weight of glory.</hi> It was the glory of Moab that their country was very populous and their forces were courageous; but where is her glory when all that great multitude is in a manner swept away, some by one judgment and some by another, and the little remnant that is left shall be <hi type="italic">very small and feeble,</hi> not able to bear up under their own griefs, much less to make head against their enemies' insults? Let not therefore the strong glory in their strength nor the many in their numbers. [2.] The time fixed for the execution of this sentence: <hi type="italic">Within three years, as the years of a hireling,</hi> that is, at the three years' end exactly, for a servant that is hired for a certain term keeps account to a day. Let Moab know that her ruin is very near, and prepare accordingly. Fair warning is given, and with it space to repent, which if they had improved, as Nineveh did, we have reason to think the judgments threatened would have been prevented.  <chapter eID="Isa.16"/> <div eID="gen15848" type="x-p"/>

entries.8a28842304b7588f963e27621e23343206ca60b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8610"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.14">Is 16:1-14</reference>. Continuation of the Prophecy as to Moab.</title> <div sID="gen14131" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8610"/><hi type="bold">1. lamb--</hi>advice of the prophet to the Moabites who had fled southwards to Idumea, to send to the king of Judah the tribute of lambs, which they had formerly paid to Israel, but which they had given up (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2Ki 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.5">5</reference>). David probably imposed this tribute before the severance of Judah and Israel (<reference osisRef="2Sam.8.2">2Sa 8:2</reference>). Therefore Moab is recommended to gain the favor and protection of Judah, by paying it to the Jewish king. Type of the need of submitting to Messiah (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.10-Ps.2.12">Psa 2:10-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.1">Ro 12:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14132" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Sela to--</hi>rather, "from Petra through (literally, 'towards') the wilderness" [Maurer]. "Sela" means "a rock," Petra in Greek; the capital of Idumea and Arabia-Petræa; the dwellings are mostly hewn out of the rock. The country around was a vast common ("wilderness") or open pasturage, to which the Moabites had fled on the invasion from the west (<reference osisRef="Isa.15.7">Is 15:7</reference>).<div eID="gen14132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14133" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ruler of the land--</hi>namely, of Idumea, that is, the king of Judah; Amaziah had become master of Idumea and Sela (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>). <div eID="gen14133" type="x-p"/>
entries.dcb98610bc1732414686e20bf7eb76eb909bbdfa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8611"/><div sID="gen14134" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8611"/><hi type="bold">2. cast out of ... nest--</hi>rather, "as a brood cast out" (in apposition with "a wandering bird," or rather, wandering birds), namely, a brood just fledged and expelled from the nest in which they were hatched [Horsley]. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Is 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">De 32:11</reference>.<div eID="gen14134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14135" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters of Moab--</hi>that is, the inhabitants of Moab. So <reference osisRef="2Kgs.19.21">2Ki 19:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.48.11">Psa 48:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.11">Jr 46:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.4.22">La 4:22</reference> [Maurer].<div eID="gen14135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14136" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at the fords--</hi>trying to cross the boundary river of Moab, in order to escape out of the land. Ewald and Maurer make "fords" a poetical expression for "the dwellers on Arnon," answering to the parallel clause of the same sense, "daughters of Moab." <div eID="gen14136" type="x-p"/>
entries.86d6020e86bfc7f2f2b5db98afcf0e505467e49f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8612"/><div sID="gen14137" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8612"/>3-5. Gesenius, Maurer, &c., regard these verses as an address of the fugitive Moabites to the Jews for protection; they translate <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Is 16:4</reference>, "Let mine outcasts of Moab dwell with thee, Judah"; the protection will be refused by the Jews, for the pride of Moab (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>). Vitringa makes it an additional advice to Moab, besides paying tribute. Give shelter to the Jewish outcasts who take refuge in thy land (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.3">Is 16:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">4</reference>); so "mercy" will be shown thee in turn by whatever king sits on the "throne" of "David" (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Is 16:5</reference>). Isaiah foresees that Moab will be too proud to pay the tribute, or conciliate Judah by sheltering its outcasts (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Is 16:6</reference>); therefore judgment shall be executed. However, as Moab just before is represented as itself an outcast in Idumea, it seems incongruous that it should be called on to shelter Jewish outcasts. So that it seems rather to foretell the ruined state of Moab when its people should beg the Jews for shelter, but be refused for their pride.<div eID="gen14137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14138" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make ... shadow as ... night ... in ... noonday--</hi>emblem of a thick shelter from the glaring noonday heat (<reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">25:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">32:2</reference>).<div eID="gen14138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14139" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bewray ... wandereth--</hi>Betray not the fugitive to his pursuer. <div eID="gen14139" type="x-p"/>
entries.41810cbe4f48d944f7ceea5738fc87ef340aea92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8615"/><div sID="gen14146" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8615"/><hi type="bold">6. We--</hi>Jews. We reject Moab's supplication for his pride.<div eID="gen14146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14147" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lies--</hi>false boasts.<div eID="gen14147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not be so--</hi>rather, "not right"; shall prove vain (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.10">Is 25:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29">Jr 48:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.30">30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8">Zep 2:8</reference>). "It shall not be so; his lies shall not so effect it." <div eID="gen14148" type="x-p"/>
entries.8b94d61f1eb53fde964baf3b1b173ff7dfcd0e91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8616"/><div sID="gen14149" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8616"/><hi type="bold">7. Therefore--</hi>all hope of being allowed shelter by the Jews being cut off.<div eID="gen14149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foundations--</hi>that is, "ruins"; because, when houses are pulled down, the "foundations" alone are left (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Is 58:12</reference>). Jeremiah, in the parallel place (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jr 48:31</reference>), renders it "men," who are the moral foundations or stay of a city.<div eID="gen14150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kirhareseth--</hi>literally, "a citadel of brick."<div eID="gen14151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14152" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">surely they are stricken--</hi>rather, joined with "mourn"; "Ye shall mourn utterly stricken" [Maurer and Horsley]. <div eID="gen14152" type="x-p"/>
entries.5e12f1d61c3457ea6eb0f60350881b7c56901801: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8617"/><div sID="gen14153" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8617"/><hi type="bold">8. fields--</hi>vine-fields (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>).<div eID="gen14153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vine of Sibmah--</hi>near Heshbon: namely, languishes.<div eID="gen14154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lords of ... heathen--</hi>The heathen princes, the Assyrians, &c., who invaded Moab, destroyed his vines. So Jeremiah in the parallel place (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jr 48:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.33">33</reference>). Maurer thinks the following words require rather the rendering, "Its (the vine of Sibmah) shoots (the wines got from them) overpowered (by its generous flavor and potency) the lords of the nations" (<reference osisRef="Gen.49.11">Ge 49:11</reference>, 12, 22).<div eID="gen14155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14156" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">come ... Jazer--</hi>They (the vine shoots) reached even to Jazer, fifteen miles from Heshbon.<div eID="gen14156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wandered--</hi>They overran in wild luxuriance the wilderness of Arabia, encompassing Moab.<div eID="gen14157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14158" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sea--</hi>the Dead Sea; or else some lake near Jazer now dry; in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jr 48:32</reference> called "the sea of Jazer"; but see on <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jr 48:32</reference> (<reference osisRef="Ps.80.8-Ps.80.11">Psa 80:8-11</reference>). <div eID="gen14158" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a2f17303a25d68bd460c30d1535286667b0360a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8618"/><div sID="gen14159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8618"/><hi type="bold">9. I--</hi>will bewail for its desolation, though I belong to another nation (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Is 15:5</reference>).<div eID="gen14159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... weeping of Jazer--</hi>as Jazer weeps.<div eID="gen14160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shouting for ... fallen--</hi>rather, "Upon thy summer fruits and upon thy luxuriant vines the shouting (the battle shout, instead of the joyous shout of the grape-gatherers, usual at the vintage) is fallen" (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">Is 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.14">51:14</reference>). In the parallel passage (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jr 48:32</reference>) the words substantially express the same sense. "The spoiler is fallen upon thy summer fruits." <div eID="gen14161" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffd2f9eb257ef34b5637853ab9ca0d1d16bb1219: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8619"/><div sID="gen14162" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8619"/><hi type="bold">10. gladness--</hi>such as is felt in gathering a rich harvest. There shall be no harvest or vintage owing to the desolation; therefore no "gladness." <div eID="gen14162" type="x-p"/>
entries.312a4afc08d4b8983472b2016cff4e9ab34fda5e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8620"/><div sID="gen14163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8620"/><hi type="bold">11. bowels--</hi>in Scripture the seat of yearning compassion. It means the inward seat of emotion, the heart, &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Is 63:15</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Is 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jr 48:36</reference>).<div eID="gen14163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sound ... harp--</hi>as its strings vibrate when beaten with the plectrum or hand. <div eID="gen14164" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed488cc1a12341d683056d2c0fcd4f832fbad4f3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8621"/><div sID="gen14165" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8621"/><hi type="bold">12. when it is seen that--</hi>rather, "When Moab shall have appeared (before his gods; compare <reference osisRef="Exod.23.15">Ex 23:15</reference>), when he is weary (that is, when he shall have fatigued himself with observing burdensome rites; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1Ki 18:26</reference>, &c.), on the high place (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.15.2">Is 15:2</reference>), and shall come to his sanctuary (of the idol Chemosh on Mount Nebo) to pray, he shall not prevail"; he shall effect nothing by his prayers [Maurer]. <div eID="gen14165" type="x-p"/>
entries.b81aae7a7406b09933549146459dfcce20bbaad8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8622"/><div sID="gen14166" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8622"/><hi type="bold">13. since that time--</hi>rather, "respecting that time" [Horsley]. Barnes translates it, "formerly" in contrast to "but now" (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Is 16:14</reference>): heretofore former prophecies (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.15">Ex 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.21.29">Nu 21:29</reference>) have been given as to Moab, of which Isaiah has given the substance: but now a definite and steady time also is fixed. <div eID="gen14166" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e78456f690bbc6aef9c954b5c4766a25c7a8677: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8623"/><div sID="gen14167" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8623"/><hi type="bold">14. three years ... hireling--</hi>Just as a hireling has his fixed term of engagement, which neither he nor his master will allow to be added to or to be taken from, so the limit within which Moab is to fall is unalterably fixed (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.16">Is 21:16</reference>). Fulfilled about the time when the Assyrians led Israel into captivity. The ruins of Elealeh, Heshbon, Medeba, Dibon, &c., still exist to confirm the inspiration of Scripture. The accurate particularity of specification of the places three thousand years ago, confirmed by modern research, is a strong testimony to the truth of prophecy. <chapter eID="Isa.16"/>

entries.dc8bd508411bf2f66073a7cccec99f7b6b729eba: <div eID="gen27176" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27177" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27178" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27177" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> The distress of Moab pathetically described by the son of the prince, or ruler of the land, being forced to flee for his life through the desert, that he may escape to Judea; and the young women, like young birds scared from their nest, wade helpless through the fords of Arnon, the boundary of their country, to seek protection in some foreign land, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Isa 16:2</reference>. The prophet addresses Sion, exhorting her to show mercy to her enemies in their distress, that her throne may be established in righteousness, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.3-Isa.16.5">Isa 16:3-5</reference>. Exceeding great pride of Moab, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference>. The terrible calamities about to fall upon Moab farther described by the languishing of the vine, the ceasing of the vintage, the sound of the prophet's bowels quivering like a harp, etc., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7-Isa.16.13">Isa 16:7-13</reference>. Awful nearness of the full accomplishment of the prophecy, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.14">Isa 16:14</reference>. <div eID="gen27179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> Send ye the lamb, etc. "I will send forth the son, etc." - Both the reading and meaning of this verse are still more doubtful than those of the preceding. The Septuagint and Syriac read אשלח eshlach, I will send, in the first person singular, future tense: the Vulgate and Talmud Babylon, read שלח shelach, send, singular imperative: some read שלחו shilchu, send ye forth, or shalechu, they send forth. The Syriac, for כר car, a lamb, reads בר bar, a son, which is confirmed by five MSS. of Kennicott and De Rossi. The two first verses describe the distress of Moab on the Assyrian invasion in which even the son of the prince of the country is represented as forced to flee for his life through the desert, that he may escape to Judea; and the young women are driven forth like young birds cast out of the nest, and endeavoring to wade through the fords of the river Arnon. Perhaps there is not so much difficulty in this verse as appears at first view. "Send the lamb to the ruler of the land," may receive light from <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2Kgs 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.5">2Kgs 3:5</reference> : "And Mesha, king of Moab, was a sheepmaster, and rendered unto the king of Israel one hundred thousand lambs with their wool, and one hundred thousand rams: but when Ahab was dead, the king of Moab rebelled against Israel." Now the prophet exhorts them to begin paying the tribute as formerly, that their punishment might be averted or mitigated.
entries.711bfd2b8b7cc801007229d9728088cb0bafafc6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen27181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> Take counsel "Impart counsel" - The Vulgate renders the verbs in the beginning of this verse in the singular number, So the Keri; and so likewise sixty-one MSS. of Kennicott's and De Rossi's have it, and nineteen editions, and the Syriac. The verbs throughout the verse are also in the feminine gender; agreeing with Zion, which I suppose to be understood.
entries.5593ce0564e69cefa8c99bc8e981c265acb2e6b4: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab "Let the outcasts of Moab sojourn with thee, O Zion" - Setting the points aside, this is by much the most obvious construction of the Hebrew, as well as most agreeable to the context, and the design of the prophet. And it is confirmed by the Septuagint οἱ φυγαδες Μωαβ, and Syriac. <div eID="gen27183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27184" type="x-p"/> The oppressors "The oppressor" - Perhaps the Israelites, who in the time of Ahab invaded Judah, defeated his army, slaying one hundred and twenty thousand men, and brought the kingdom to the brink of destruction. Judah, being now in a more prosperous condition, is represented as able to receive and to protect the fugitive Moabites. And with those former times of distress the security and flourishing state of the kingdom under the government of Hezekiah is contrasted.
entries.bf5d49e147c9c32273411141abf1016ffb70de7e: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27185" type="x-p"/> In mercy shall the throne be established - May not this refer to the throne of Hezekiah? Here we have the character of such a king as cannot fail to be a blessing to the people. <div eID="gen27185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27186" type="x-p"/> 1. "He sitteth on the throne in truth" - He does not merely profess to be the father and protector of his people: but he is actually such. <div eID="gen27186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27187" type="x-p"/> 2. He is judging. He is not a man of war or blood, who wastes his subjects' lives and treasures in contentions with neighboring nations, in order to satisfy his ambition by the extension of his territory. On the contrary, his whole life is occupied in the distribution of justice. <div eID="gen27187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> 3. He seeketh judgment. He seeks out the poor distressed ones who cannot make their way to him, and avenges them on their oppressors. <div eID="gen27188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> 4. He hastens righteousness. He does not suffer any of the courts of justice to delay the determination of the causes brought before them: he so orders that the point in litigation be fairly, fully, and speedily heard; and then judgment pronounced. Delays in the execution of justice answer little end but the enriching of unprincipled lawyers.
entries.81d1e08d71979e3f4de5fc4795af965ddefed070: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> We have heard of the pride of Moab "We have heard the pride of Moab" - For גא ge, read גאה geah; two MSS., one ancient, and <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29">Jer 48:29</reference>. Zephaniah, <reference osisRef="Zep.2.8-Zep.2.10">Zep 2:8-10</reference>, in his prophecy against Moab, the subject of which is the same with that of Jeremiah in his forty-eighth chapter, (see the note on <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference> (note)), enlarges much on the pride of Moab, and their insolent behavior towards the Jews: - "I have heard the reproach of Moab; <div eID="gen27190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> And the revilings of the sons of Ammon: <div eID="gen27191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> Who have reproached my people; <div eID="gen27192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> And have magnified themselves against their borders. <div eID="gen27193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> Therefore, as I live, saith Jehovah God of hosts, the God of Israel: <div eID="gen27194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> Surely Moab shall be as Sodom, <div eID="gen27195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> And the sons of Ammon as Gomorrah: <div eID="gen27196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> A possession of nettles, and pits of salt, <div eID="gen27197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> And a desolation for ever. <div eID="gen27198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> The residue of my people shall spoil them, <div eID="gen27199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> And the remnant of my nation shall dispossess them: <div eID="gen27200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> This shall they have for their pride; <div eID="gen27201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27202" type="x-p"/> Because they have raised a reproach, and have magnified themselves <div eID="gen27202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> Against the people of Jehovah God of hosts."
entries.947d8821f2dca85bd9c9f3e90031b6c47df4532d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> For the foundations of Kir-hareseth "For the men of Kirhares" - A palpable mistake in this place is happily corrected by the parallel text of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jer 48:31</reference>, where, instead of אשישי ashishey, foundations or flagons, we read אנשי anshey, men. In the same place of Jeremiah, and in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference>, and here in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Isa 16:11</reference>, the name of the city is Kirhares, not Kirhareseth.
entries.9bd8f0a8a64130d55789f0eeb67846c480847e75: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27205" type="x-p"/> Languish "Are put to shame" - Here the text of Jeremiah leaves us much at a loss, in a place that seems to be greatly corrupted. The Septuagint join the two last words of this verse with the beginning of the following. Their rendering is: και ουκ εντραπησῃ, τα πεδια Εσεβων. For אך ach they must have read אל al; otherwise, how came they by the negative, which seems not to belong to this place? Neither is it easy to make sense of the rest without a small alteration, by reading, instead of εντραπησῃ τα, εντραπησεται. In a word, the Arabic version taken from the Septuagint, plainly authorizes this reading of the Septuagint, and without the negative; and it is fully confirmed by MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. II., which have both of them εντραπησεται πεδια Εσεβων, without the negative; which makes an excellent sense, and, I think, gives us the true reading of the Hebrew text; אך נכלמו שדמות חשבון ak nichlemu shadmoth cheshbon. They frequently render the verb נכלם nichlam by εντρεπομαι. And נכלמו nichlemu answers perfectly well to אמלל umlal, the parallel word in the next line. The MSS. vary in expressing the word נכאים nechaim, which gives no tolerable sense in this place; one reads נוכאים nochaim; two others בכאים bechaim; in another the כ caph is upon a rasure of two letters; and the Vulgate instead of it reads מכותם mecotham, plagas suas. - L. <div eID="gen27205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27206" type="x-p"/> For the men of Kirhares ye shall make a moan. For the fields of Heshbon are put to shame. This is Bp. Lowth's sense of the passage. <div eID="gen27206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27207" type="x-p"/> Her branches are stretched out "Her branches extended themselves" - For נטשו nitteshu, a MS. has נגשו niggeshu; which may perhaps be right. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>, which has in this part of the sentence the synonymous word נגעו nagau. <div eID="gen27207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> The meaning of this verse is, that the wines of Sibmah and Heshbon were greatly celebrated, and in high repute with all the great men and princes of that and the neighboring countries; who indulged themselves even to intemperance in the use of them. So that their vines were so much in request as not only to be propagated all over the country of Moab to the sea of Sodom, but to have scions of them sent even beyond the sea into foreign countries. הלמו halemu, knocked down, demolished; that is overpowered, intoxicated. The drunkards of Ephraim are called by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>, הלומי יין halumey yayin, drinkers of wine. See Schultens on <reference osisRef="Pro.23.25">Pro 23:25</reference>. Gratius, speaking of the Mareotic wine, says of it, <div eID="gen27208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> Pharios quae fregit noxia reges. Cyneg. 312.
entries.2cb4e94506c3d6989bcdab91858abe961a7d48d1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen27209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27210" type="x-p"/> With the weeping "As with the weeping" - For בבכי bibechi, a MS. reads בכי bechi. In <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>, it is מבכי mibbechi. The Septuagint read כבכי kibeki, as with weeping, which I follow. <div eID="gen27210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> For thy summer fruits and for thy harvest is fallen "And upon thy vintage the destroyer hath fallen" - ועל קצירך הידד נפל veal ketsirech heidad naphal. In these few words there are two great mistakes, which the text of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference> rectifies. For קצירך ketsirech, it has בצירך betsirech; and for הידד heidad, שדד shoded; both which corrections the Chaldee in this place confirms. As to the first, "Hesebon and Eleale, and <div eID="gen27211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> The flowery dale of Sibmah, clad with vines," were never celebrated for their harvests; it was the vintage that suffered by the irruption of the enemy; and so read the Septuagint and Syriac. הידד heidad is the noisy acclamation of the treaders of the grapes. And see what sense this makes in the literal rendering of the Vulgate: super messem tuam vox calcantium irruit, "upon thy harvest the voice of the treaders rushes." The reading in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference> is certainly right, שדד נפל shoded naphal, "the destroyer hath fallen." The shout of the treaders does not come in till the next verse; in which the text of Isaiah in its turn mends that of <reference osisRef="Jer.48.33">Jer 48:33</reference>, where instead of the first הידד heidad, "the shout," we ought undoubtedly to read, as here, הדרך haddorech, "the treader."
entries.9d86f4af5ee966b6125b52ba6416226e85470013: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen27212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27213" type="x-p"/> Neither shall there be shouting "An end is put to the shouting" - The Septuagint read השבת hishbeth, passive, and in the third person; rightly, for God is not the speaker in this place. The rendering of the Septuagint is πεπαυται γαρ κελευσμα, "the cry ceaseth;" which last word, necessary to the rendering of the Hebrew and to the sense, is supplied by MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. II., having been lost out of the other copies.
entries.a3b507137055817f1321a6677becf1da7a768464: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen27213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27214" type="x-p"/> When it is seen that Moab, etc. "When Moab shall see," etc. - For נראה nirah, a MS. reads ראה raah, and so the Syriac and Chaldee. "Perhaps כי נראה ki nirah is only a various reading of כי נלאה ki nilah." Secker. A very probable conjecture.
entries.efd2e5f0856e33d3db8cf83449f2f0c3d4f44f20: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen27214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27215" type="x-p"/> Within three years - בשלש beshalish כשלש keshalish, according, or in or about three years, is the reading of nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and two ancient editions. <div eID="gen27215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27216" type="x-p"/> But the present reading may well stand: "Now, the Lord hath spoken, saying, Within three years, as the years of a hireling." It seems as if this prophecy had been delivered before, without any time specified for its fulfillment; but now the time is determined" in three years, as the years of a hireling" - for, as a hireling counts even to a single day, and will not abide with his employer an hour beyond the time agreed on; so, in three years, even to a day, from the delivery of this prophecy, shall destruction come upon Moab. This is the import of the present text; but if we take כשלש keshalish, AS in three years, or in about three years' time, the prophecy is not so definite. <div eID="gen27216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27217" type="x-p"/> These three years, says Calmet, are mentioned from the death of Ahaz, see <reference osisRef="Isa.14.28">Isa 14:28</reference>, and end the third year of Hezekiah, three years before the taking of Samaria by Shalmaneser. This conqueror did not ruin Moab so completely as not to leave a man in the land; the final desolation of Moab was reserved for Nebuchadnezzar, five years after the taking of Jerusalem. <div eID="gen27217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27218" type="x-p"/> Feeble "And without strength" - An ancient MS., with the Septuagint, reads ולא velo, "and not."  <chapter eID="Isa.16"/> <div eID="gen27218" type="x-p"/>

entries.ea29a9d9ed9cb3894b659e8d73b44696a2fd977e: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference> <div eID="gen13017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13018" type="x-p"/> But just because this lion is Judah and its government, the summons goes forth to the Moabites, who have fled to Edom, and even to <hi type="italic">Sela</hi>, i.e., Petra (<hi type="italic">Wady Musa</hi>), near Mount Hor in Arabia Petraea, to which it gave its name, to turn for protection to Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">“Send a land-ruler’s tribute of lambs from Sela desert-wards to the mountain of the daughter of Zion.”</hi> This v. is like a long-drawn trumpet-blast. The prophecy against Moab takes the same turn here as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.32">Isa 14:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference>; Isa 19:16., Isa 23:18. The judgment first of all produces slavish fear; and this is afterwards refined into loving attachment. Submission to the house of David is Moab’s only deliverance. This is what the prophet, weeping with those that weep, calls out to them in such long-drawn, vehement, and urgent tones, even into the farthest hiding-place in which they have concealed themselves, viz., the rocky city of the Edomites. The tribute of lambs which was due to the ruling prince is called briefly <hi type="italic">car mōshēl</hi>-<hi type="italic">'eretz</hi>. This tribute, which the holders of the pasture-land so rich in flocks have hitherto sent to Samaria (2Ki 3:4), they are now to send to Jerusalem, the “mountain of the daughter of Zion” (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference>), the way to which lay through “<hi type="italic">the desert</hi>,” i.e., first of all in a diagonal direction through the Arabah, which stretched downwards to Aelath.
entries.71afbf65eee21e12b6db3a14652d28d5f7826ee3: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.2">Isa 16:2</reference> <div eID="gen13018" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13019" type="x-p"/> The advice does not remain without effect, but they embrace it eagerly.<hi type="italic">”And the daughters of Moab will be like birds fluttering about, a scared nest, at the fords of the Arnon.”</hi> “The daughters of Moab,” like “the daughters of Judah,” for example, in <reference osisRef="Ps.48.12">Psa 48:12</reference>, are the inhabitants of the cities and villages of the land of Moab. They were already like birds soaring about (<reference osisRef="Prov.27.8">Pro 27:8</reference>), because of their flight from their own land; but here, as we may see from the expression תהיינה ... והיה, the simile is intended to depict the condition into which they would be thrown by the prophet’s advice. The figure (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.14">Isa 10:14</reference>) as well as the expression (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.17.2">Isa 17:2</reference>) is thoroughly Isaiah's. It is a state of anxious and timid indecision, resembling the fluttering to and fro of birds, that have been driven away from their nest, and wheel anxiously round and round, without daring to return to their old home. In this way the daughters of Moab, coming out of their hiding-places, whether nearer or more remote, show themselves at the fords of the Arnon, that is to say, on the very soil of their old home, which was situated between the Arnon and Wady el-Ahsa, and which was now devastated by the hand of a foe. לארנון מעברות we should regard as in apposition to <hi type="italic">benoth Moab</hi> (the daughters of Moab), if <hi type="italic">ma‛bâroth</hi> signifies the coast-lands (like <hi type="italic">‛ebrē</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.7.20">Isa 7:20</reference>), and not, as it invariably does, the fords. It is locative in its meaning, and is so accentuated.
entries.bc9e304564d7f98312af7fd3fc86cd1e774d79f6: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.3-Isa.16.5">Isa 16:3-5</reference> <div eID="gen13019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13020" type="x-p"/> There they show themselves, on the spot to which their land once reached before it passed into the possession of Israel - <hi type="italic">there</hi>, on its farthest boundary in the direction towards Judah, which was seated above; and taking heart, address the following petitions to Zion, or to the Davidic court, on the other side. <hi type="italic">“Give counsel, form a decision, make thy shadow like night in the midst of noon; hide the outcasts, do not betray the wanderers. Let mine outcasts tarry in thee, Moab; be a covert to it from before the spoiler.”</hi> In their extremity they appeal to Zion for counsel, and the once proud but now thoroughly humbled Moabites place the decision of their fate in the hands of the men of Judah (so according to the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>), and stand before Zion praying most earnestly for shelter and protection. Their fear of the enemy is so great, that in the light of the noon-day sun they desire to be covered with the protecting shade of Zion as with the blackness of night, that they may not be seen by the foe. The short-sentences correspond to the anxious urgency of the prayer (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.8">Isa 33:8</reference>). <hi type="italic">Pelilâh</hi> (cf., <hi type="italic">peililyyâh</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.7">Isa 28:7</reference>) is the decision of a judge (<hi type="italic">pâlil</hi>); just as in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference> <hi type="italic">sheilshiyyâh</hi> is the age and standing of three years. The figure of the shadow is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.2-Isa.30.3">Isa 30:2-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>, etc.; <hi type="italic">nōdēd</hi> is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.14">Isa 21:14</reference>; <hi type="italic">niddâchai</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa 11:12</reference>; <hi type="italic">sēther</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference>, and other passages; <hi type="italic">shōdēd</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>; <hi type="italic">mippenē</hi> as in Isa 21:15. The whole is word for word Isaiah's. There is no necessity to read <hi type="italic">nidchē</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">niddâc</hi> <hi type="italic">Mo'âb</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Isa 16:4</reference>; still less is ay a collective termination, as in Isa 20:4. Nor are the words to be rendered “my outcasts ... of Moab,” and the expression to be taken as a <hi type="italic">syntaxis ornata</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.17.6">Isa 17:6</reference>). On the contrary, such an expression is absolutely impossible here, where the speaker is alluding to himself. It is better to abide by the punctuation as we have it, with <hi type="italic">niddâchai</hi> (<hi type="italic">zakeph</hi>) closing the first clause of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Isa 16:4</reference></hi>, and Moab (<hi type="italic">tebir</hi>, which is subordinate to the following <hi type="italic">tiphchah</hi>, and with this to <hi type="italic">athnach</hi>) opening the second as an absolute noun. This is the way in which we have rendered it above: “Moab ... be a shield to it ... ” (though without taking <hi type="italic">lâmō</hi> as equivalent to <hi type="italic">lō</hi>). <div eID="gen13020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13021" type="x-p"/> The question then arises, By what means has Zion awakened such reverence and confidence on the part of Moab? This question is answered in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Isa 16:4</reference></hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.5">Isa 16:5</reference> : <hi type="italic">“For the extortioner is at an end, desolation has disappeared, treaders down are away from the land. And a throne is established by grace, and there sits thereon in truth in the tent of David one judging, and zealous for right, and practised in righteousness.”</hi> The imperial world-power, which pressed out both marrow and blood (<hi type="italic">mētz</hi>, a noun of the same form as <hi type="italic">lētz</hi>, like <hi type="italic">mı̄tz</hi> in <reference osisRef="Prov.30.33">Pro 30:33</reference>, pressure), and devastated and trod down everything (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.20">Isa 29:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.1">Isa 33:1</reference>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>), is swept away from the land on this side of the Jordan; Jerusalem is not subject to it now, but has come forth more gloriously out of all her oppressions than ever she did before. And the throne of the kingdom of Judah has not fallen down, but by the manifestation of Jehovah’s grace has been newly established. There no longer sits thereon a king who dishonours Him, and endangers His kingdom; but the tent-roof of the fallen and now re-erected hut of David (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Amo 9:11</reference>) is spread over a King in whom the truth of the promise of Jehovah is verified, inasmuch as justice and righteousness are realized through all that He does. The Messianic times must therefore have dawned (so the Targum understands it), since grace and truth (<hi type="italic">chesed ve'emeth</hi>) and “justice and righteousness” (<hi type="italic">mishpât</hi> <hi type="italic">ūtzedâkâh</hi>) are the divino-human signs of those times, and as it were their kindred genii; and who can here fail to recall to mind the words of <reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa 9:6</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5-Isa.33.6">Isa 33:5-6</reference>)? The king depicted here is the same as “the lion out of Judah,” threatened against Moab in Isa 15:9. Only by thus submitting to Him and imploring His grace will it escape the judgment.
entries.ff44fac5b6fa0f09c7748a27794894037de6af25: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference> <div eID="gen13021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13022" type="x-p"/> But if Moab does this, and the law of the history of Israel, which is that “a remnant shall return,” is thus reflected in the history of Moab; <reference osisRef="Isa.16.6">Isa 16:6</reference> cannot possibly contain the answer which Moab receives from Zion, as the more modern commentators assume according to an error that has almost become traditional. On the contrary, the prophecy enters here upon a new stage, commencing with Moab’s sin, and depicting the fate of Moab in still more elegiac strains. <hi type="italic">“We have heard of the pride of Moab, the very haughty </hi>(<hi type="italic">pride</hi>)<hi type="italic">, his haughtiness, and his pride, and his wrath, the falsehood of his speech.”</hi> The future self-humiliation of Moab, which would be the fruit of its sufferings, is here contrasted with the previous self-exaltation, of which these sufferings were the fruit. “<hi type="italic">We have heard</hi>,” says the prophet, identifying himself with his people. Boasting pompousness has hitherto been the distinguishing characteristic of Moab in relation to the latter (see <reference osisRef="Isa.25.11">Isa 25:11</reference>). The heaping up of words of the same verbal stem (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.3.1">Isa 3:1</reference>) is here intended to indicate how thoroughly haughty was their haughtiness (cf., <reference osisRef="Rom.7.13">Rom 7:13</reference>, “that sin might become exceeding sinful”), and how completely it had taken possession of Moab. It boasted and was full of rage towards Israel, to which, so far as it retained its consciousness of the truth of Jehovah, the talk of Moab (בדיו from בדד = בדא, בטא, to talk at random) must necessarily appear as לא־כן, <hi type="italic">not-right</hi>, i.e., at variance with fact. These expressions of opinion had been heard by the people of God, and, as Jeremiah adds in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.29-Jer.48.30">Jer 48:29-30</reference>, by Israel’s God as well.
entries.ee36d1aaecb626692d5fbfe1640afe61764d7aae: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.7-Isa.16.8">Isa 16:7-8</reference> <div eID="gen13022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13023" type="x-p"/> Therefore the delightful land is miserably laid waste. <hi type="italic">“Therefore will Moab wail for Moab, everything will wail: for the grape-cakes of Kir-hareseth will ye whine, utterly crushed. For the fruit-fields of Heshbon have faded away: the vine of Sibmah, lords of the nations its branches smote down; they reached to Ja'zer, trailed through the desert: its branches spread themselves out wide, crossed over the sea.”</hi> The <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> in <hi type="italic">l'Moab</hi> is the same as in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference>, and in <hi type="italic">la'ashishē</hi>, which follows here. <hi type="italic">Kir</hi>-<hi type="italic">hareseth</hi> (written <hi type="italic">Kir</hi>-<hi type="italic">heres</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.11">Isa 16:11</reference>, and by Jeremiah; compare 2Ki 3:25, where the vowel-pointing is apparently false): <hi type="italic">Heres</hi> or <hi type="italic">Hareseth</hi> may possibly refer to the glazed tiles or grooved stones. As this was the principal fortress of Moab, and according to <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference> it had already been destroyed, <hi type="italic">‛ashishē</hi> appears to mean the “strong foundations,” - namely, as laid bare; in other words, the “ruins” (cf., <reference osisRef="Jer.50.15">Jer 50:15</reference>, and <hi type="italic">mōsedē</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>). But in every other passage in which the word occurs it signifies a kind of cake; and as the devastation of the vines of Moab is made the subject of mourning afterwards, it has the same meaning here as in Hos 3:1, namely <hi type="italic">raisin-cakes</hi>, or raisins pressed into the form of cakes. Such cakes as these may have been a special article of the export trade of Kir. Jeremiah has altered <hi type="italic">'ashishē</hi> into <hi type="italic">'anshē</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.31">Jer 48:31</reference>), and thus made men out of the grapes. <hi type="italic">Hâgâh</hi> is to be understood in accordance with <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa 38:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">Isa 59:11</reference> (viz., of the cooing of the dove); <hi type="italic">'ac</hi> (in good texts it is written with <hi type="italic">mercha</hi>, not with <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>) according to Deu 16:15. On the construction of the <hi type="italic">pluralet</hi>. <hi type="italic">shadmoth</hi>, compare Hab 3:17. We have rendered the clause commencing with <hi type="italic">baalē goyim</hi> (lords of the nations) with the same amphibolism as we find in the Hebrew. It might mean either “lords of the nations (<hi type="italic">domini gentium</hi>) smote down its branches” (viz., those of the vine of <hi type="italic">Sibmah</hi>;<note placement="foot">In MSS Shibmah is written with <hi type="italic">gaya</hi>, in order that the two labials may be distinctly expressed.</note><hi type="italic">hâlam</hi> being used as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.7">Isa 41:7</reference>), or “its branches smote down (i.e., intoxicated) lords of the nations” (<hi type="italic">dominos gentium</hi>; <hi type="italic">hâlam</hi> having the same meaning as in the undisputed prophecy of Isaiah in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">Isa 28:1</reference>). As the prophet enlarges here upon the excellence of the Moabitish wine, the latter is probably intended. The wine of Sibmah was so good, that it was placed upon the tables of monarchs, and so strong that it smote down, i.e., inevitably intoxicated, even those who were accustomed to good wines. This Sibmah wine was cultivated, as the prophet says, far and wide in Moab - northwards as far as <hi type="italic">Ja'zer</hi> (between Ramoth, i.e., Salt, and Heshbon, now a heap of ruins), eastwards into the desert, and southwards across the Dead Sea - a hyperbolical expression for close up to its shores. Jeremiah defines <hi type="italic">yâm</hi> (the sea) more closely as <hi type="italic">yam Ja‛zer</hi> (the sea of Jazer; vid., <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>), so that the hyperbole vanishes. But what sea can the sea of Jazer be? Probably some celebrated large pool, like the pools of Heshbon, in which the waters of the <hi type="italic">Wady</hi> (<hi type="italic">Nahr</hi>) <hi type="italic">Sir</hi>, which takes its rise close by, were collected. Seetzen found some pools still there. The “sea” (<hi type="italic">yâm</hi>) in Solomon’s temple shows clearly enough that the term sea was also commonly applied to artificial basins of a large size; and in Damascus the marble basins of flowing water in the halls of houses are still called <hi type="italic">baharât</hi>; and the same term is applied to the public reservoirs in all the streets of the city, which are fed by a network of aqueducts from the river <hi type="italic">Baradâ</hi>. The expression “break through the desert” (<hi type="italic">tâ‛u</hi> <hi type="italic">midbâr</hi>) is also a bold one, probably pointing to the fact that, like the red wines of Hungary at the present time, they were trailing vines, which did not require to be staked, but ran along the ground.
entries.09df7d916a4712d0951eec6acfdf51eda90f0ee6: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference> <div eID="gen13023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13024" type="x-p"/> The beauties of nature and fruitfulness of the land, which come into the possession of any nation, are gifts from the riches of divine goodness, remnants of the paradisaical commencement of the history of man, and types of its paradisaical close; and for this very reason they are not matters of indifference to the spirit of prophecy. And for the same reason, it is not unworthy of a prophet, who predicts the renovation of nature and the perfecting of it into the beauty of paradise, to weep over such a devastation as that of the Moabitish vineyards which was now passing before his mind (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.32.12-Isa.32.13">Isa 32:12-13</reference>).<hi type="italic">“Therefore I bemoan the vines of Sibmah with the weeping of Jazer; I flood thee with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh, that Hêdad hath fallen upon thy fruit-harvest and upon thy vintage.”</hi> A tetrastich, the Hebrew equivalent, in measure and movement, of a sapphic strophe. The circumstantiality of the vision is here swallowed up again by the sympathy of the prophet; and the prophecy, which is throughout as truly human as it is divine, becomes soft and flowing like an elegy. The prophet mingles his tears with the tears of Jazer. Just as the latter weeps for the devastated vines of <hi type="italic">Sibmah</hi>, so does he also weep. The form אריּוך, transposed from ארוּיך = ארוּך (cf., Ewald, §253, a, where it is explained as being a rare “voluntative” formation), corresponds to the elegiac tone of the whole strophe. <hi type="italic">Heshbon</hi> and <hi type="italic">Elealeh</hi>, those closely connected cities, with their luxuriant fields (<hi type="italic">shedemoth</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>), are now lying in ruins; and the prophet waters them with tears, because <hi type="italic">hedad</hi> has fallen upon the fruit-harvest and vintage of both the sister cities. In other instances the term <hi type="italic">kâtzı̄r</hi> is applied to the <hi type="italic">wheat-harvest</hi>; but here it is used in the same sense as <hi type="italic">bâtzı̄r</hi>, to which it is preferred on account of Isaiah’s favourite alliteration, viz., with <hi type="italic">kaytz</hi> (compare, for example, the alliteration of <hi type="italic">mistor</hi> with <hi type="italic">sēther</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Isa 4:6</reference>). That it does not refer to the wheat-harvest here, but to the vintage, which was nearly coincident with the fruit-harvest (which is called <hi type="italic">kaytz</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.4">Isa 28:4</reference>), is evident from the figure suggested in the word <hi type="italic">hēdâd</hi>, which was the shout raised by the pressers of the grapes, to give the time for moving their feet when treading out the wine (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.10">Isa 16:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jer 25:30</reference>). A <hi type="italic">hēdâd</hi> of this kind had fallen upon the rich floors of Heshbon-Elealeh, inasmuch as they had been trodden down by enemies - a <hi type="italic">Hedad</hi>, and yet no <hi type="italic">Hedad</hi>, as Jeremiah gives it in a beautiful oxymoron (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.33">Jer 48:33</reference>), i.e., no joyous shout of actual grape-treaders.
entries.3127ec68ae53cd0467692bac7874d97003fa35b0: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.10-Isa.16.11">Isa 16:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen13024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13025" type="x-p"/> The prophet, to whose favourite words and favourite figures Carmel belongs, both as the name of a place and as the name of a thing, now proceeds with his picture, and is plunged still more deeply into mourning. <hi type="italic">“And joy is taken away, and the rejoicing of the garden-land; and there is no exulting, no shouting in the vineyards: the treader treads out no wine in the presses; I put an end to the Hedad. Therefore my bowels sound for Moab like a harp, and my inside for Kir-heres.”</hi> It is Jehovah who says “I put an end;” and consequently the words, “My bowels sound like a harp,” or, as Jeremiah expresses it (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.36">Jer 48:36</reference>), like flutes, might appear to be expressive of the feelings of Jehovah. And the Scriptures do not hesitate to attribute <hi type="italic">mē‛ayim</hi> (<hi type="italic">viscera</hi>) to God (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.63.15">Isa 63:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer 31:20</reference>). But as the prophet is the sympathizing subject throughout the whole of the prophecy, it is better, for the sake of unity, to take the words in this instance also as expressing the prophet’s feelings. Just as the hand or <hi type="italic">plectrum</hi> touches the strings of the harp, so that they vibrate with sound; so did the terrible things that he had heard Jehovah say concerning Moab touch the strings of his inward parts, and cause them to resound with notes of pain. By the bowels, or rather entrails (<hi type="italic">viscera</hi>), the heart, liver, and kidneys are intended - the highest organs of the Psyche, and the sounding-board, as it were, of those “hidden sounds” which exist in every man. God conversed with the prophet “in the spirit;” but what passed there took the form of individual impressions in the domain of the soul, in which impressions the bodily organs of the psychical life sympathetically shared. Thus the prophet saw in the spirit the purpose of God concerning Moab, in which he could not and would not make any change; but it threw his soul into all the restlessness of pain.
