entries.6afd1f6f9e46a3fb512a8e7abfcb25b2c64f334f: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.12">Isa 16:12</reference> <div eID="gen13025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13026" type="x-p"/> The ultimate reason for this restlessness is, that Moab does not know the living God. <hi type="italic">“And it will come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary with weeping upon the mountain height, and enters into its sanctuary to pray, it will not gain anything.”</hi> נלאה נראה, a pictorial assonance, such as Isaiah delights in. נראה .ni st is transferred from the Israelitish worship (appearance before God in His temple) to the heathen; syntactically, <hi type="italic">si apparuerit</hi>, etc., with <hi type="italic">Vav</hi> before the apodosis. It would be with the Moabites as with the priests of Baal in the time of Elijah (1Ki 18:26.).
entries.94c58cc6e2517e22c5184f6329d2d5b2f7030d91: <reference osisRef="Isa.16.13-Isa.16.14">Isa 16:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen13026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13027" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">massa</hi> is now brought to a close, and there follows an epilogue which fixes the term of the fulfilment of what is not predicted now for the first time, from the standpoint of the anticipated history. <hi type="italic">“This is the word which Jehovah spake long ago concerning Moab. And now Jehovah speaketh thus: In three years, like years of a hireling, the glory of Moab is disgraced, together with all the multitude of the great; a remnant is left, contemptibly small, not great at all.”</hi> The time fixed is the same as in Isa 20:3. Of working time the hirer remits nothing, and the labourer gives nothing in. The statement as to the time, therefore, is intended to be taken exactly: three years, not more, rather under than over. Then will the old saying of God concerning Moab be fulfilled. Only a remnant, a contemptible remnant, will be left (וּשׁאר, cf., וּמשׂושׂ, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.6">Isa 8:6</reference>, in sense equivalent to ושׁאר); for every history of the nations is but the shadow of the history of Israel. <div eID="gen13027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13028" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">massa</hi> in Isaiah 15:1-16:12 was a word that had already gone forth from Jehovah “long ago.” This statement may be understood in three different senses. In the <hi type="italic">first</hi> place, Isaiah may mean that older prophecies had already foretold essentially the same concerning Moab. But what prophecies? We may get an answer to this question from the prophecies of Jeremiah concerning Moab in Jer 48. Jeremiah there reproduces the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> <hi type="italic">Moab</hi> of the book of Isaiah, but interweaves with it reminiscences (1.) out of the <hi type="italic">mâshal</hi> on Moab in Num 21:27-30; (2.) out of Balaam’s prophecy concerning Moab in Num 24:17; (3.) out of the prophecy of Amos concerning Moab (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.1-Amos.2.3">Amo 2:1-3</reference>). And it might be to these earlier words of prophecy that Isaiah here refers (Hävernick, Drechsler, and others). But this is very improbable, as there is no ring of these earlier passages in the <hi type="italic">massa</hi>, such as we should expect if Isaiah had had them in his mind. <hi type="italic">Secondly</hi>, Isaiah might mean that Isa 15:1. contained the prophecy of an older prophet, which he merely brought to remembrance in order to connect therewith the precise tenor of its fulfilment which had been revealed to him. This is at present the prevailing view. Hitzig, in a special work on the subject (1831), as well as in his Commentary, has endeavoured to prove, on the ground of 2Ki 14:25, that in all probability <hi type="italic">Jonah</hi> was the author of the oracle which Isaiah here resumes. And Knobel, Maurer, Gustav Baur, and Thenius agree with him in this; whilst De Wette, Ewald, and Umbreit regard it as, at any rate, decidedly non-Messianic. If the conjecture that Jonah was the author could but be better sustained, we should heartily rejoice in this addition to the history of the literature of the Old Testament. But all that we know of Jonah is at variance with such a conjecture. He was a prophet of the type of Elijah and Elisha, in whom the eloquence of a prophet’s words was thrown altogether into the shade by the energy of a prophet’s deeds. His prophecy concerning the restoration of the kingdom of Israel to its old boundaries, which was fulfilled by the victories of Jeroboam II, we cannot therefore imagine to have been so pictorial or highly poetical as the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> <hi type="italic">Moab</hi> (which would only be one part of that prophecy) really is; and the fact that he was angry at the sparing of Nineveh harmonizes very badly with its elegiac softness and its flood of tears. Moreover, it is never intimated that the conquerors to whom Moab was to succumb would belong to the kingdom of Israel; and the hypothesis is completely overthrown by the summons addressed to Moab to send tribute to Jerusalem. But the conclusion itself, that the oracle must have originated with any older prophet whatever, is drawn from very insufficient premises. No doubt it is a thing altogether unparalleled even in Isaiah, that a prophecy should assume so thoroughly the form of a <hi type="italic">kinah</hi>, or lamentation; still there are tendencies to this in <reference osisRef="Isa.22.4">Isa 22:4</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3-Isa.21.4">Isa 21:3-4</reference>), and Isaiah was an inexhaustible master of language of every character and colour. It is true we do light upon many expressions which cannot be pointed out anywhere else in the book of Isaiah, such as <hi type="italic">baalē</hi> <hi type="italic">goyim</hi>, <hi type="italic">hedâd</hi>, <hi type="italic">yelâlâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">yâra‛</hi>, <hi type="italic">yithrâh</hi>, <hi type="italic">mâhir</hi>, <hi type="italic">mētz</hi>, <hi type="italic">nosâphoth</hi>, <hi type="italic">pekuddâh</hi> (provision, possession); and there is something peculiar in the circular movement of the prophecy, which is carried out to such an extent in the indication of reason and consequence, as well as in the perpetually returning, monotonous connection of the sentences by <hi type="italic">ci</hi> (for) and <hi type="italic">‛al</hi>-<hi type="italic">cēn</hi> (<hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi>, therefore), the former of which is repeated twice in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.1">Isa 15:1</reference>, three times in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.8-Isa.15.9">Isa 15:8-9</reference>, and four times in succession in <reference osisRef="Isa.15.5">Isa 15:5</reference>-6. But there is probably no prophecy, especially in chapters 13-23, which does not contain expressions that the prophet uses nowhere else; and so far as the conjunctions <hi type="italic">ci</hi> and <hi type="italic">a‛ l</hi>-<hi type="italic">cēn</hi> (<hi type="italic">lâcēn</hi>), are concerned, Isaiah crowds them together in other passages as well, and here almost to monotony, as a natural consequence of the prevailing elegiac tone. Besides, even Ewald can detect the characteristics of Isaiah in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1-Isa.16.6">Isa 16:1-6</reference>; and you have only to dissect the whole rhetorically, syntactically, and philologically, with the carefulness of a Caspari, to hear throughout the ring of Isaiah’s style. And whoever has retained the impression which he brought with him from the oracle against Philistia, will be constrained to say, that not only the stamp and outward form, but also the spirit and ideas, are thoroughly Isaiah's. Hence the third possible conjecture must be the correct one. <hi type="italic">Thirdly</hi>, then, Isaiah may mean that the fate of Moab, which he has just proclaimed, was revealed to him long ago; and the addition made now is, that it will be fulfilled in exactly three years. מאז does not necessarily point to a time antecedent to that of Isaiah himself (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.44.8">Isa 44:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.3">Isa 48:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.5">Isa 48:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.48.7">Isa 48:7</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.34">2Sa 15:34</reference>). If we assume that what Isaiah predicts down to <reference osisRef="Isa.16.12">Isa 16:12</reference> was revealed to him in the year that Ahaz died, and that the epilogue reckons from the third or tenth year of Hezekiah, in either case the interval is long enough for the <hi type="italic">mê'âz</hi> (from of old). And we decide in favour of this. Unfortunately, we know nothing certain as to the time at which the three years commence. The question whether it was Shalmanassar, Sargon, or Sennacherib who treated the Moabites so harshly, is one that we cannot answer. In Herodotus (ii. 141), Sennacherib is called “king of the Arabians and Assyrians;” and Moab might be included in the Arabians. In any case, after the fulfilment of Isaiah’s prophecy in the Assyrian times, there was still a portion left, the fulfilment of which, according to Jer 48, was reserved for the Chaldeans. The Oracle Concerning Damascus and Israel - <reference osisRef="Isa.17.1-Isa.17.14">Isa 17:1-14</reference> <div eID="gen13028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13029" type="x-p"/> From the Philistines on the west, and the Moabites on the east, the prophecy relating to the neighbouring nations now turns, without any chronological order, to the people of Damascene Syria on the north. The curse pronounced on them, however, falls upon the kingdom of Israel also, because it has allied itself with heathen Damascus, in opposition to its own brother tribe to the south, as well as to the Davidic government; and by this unnatural alliance with a <hi type="italic">zâr</hi>, or stranger, had become a <hi type="italic">zâr</hi> itself. From the period of Hezekiah’s reign, to which the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> <hi type="italic">Moab</hi> belongs, at least so far as its epilogue is concerned, we are here carried back to the reign of Ahaz, and indeed far beyond “the year that Ahaz died” (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.28">Isa 14:28</reference>), to the very border of the reigns of Jotham and Ahaz - namely, to the time when the league for the destruction of Judah had only just been concluded. At the time when Isaiah incorporated this oracle in his collection, the threats against the kingdoms of Damascus and Israel had long been fulfilled. Assyria had punished both of them. And Assyria itself had also been punished, as the fourth turn in the oracle indicates. Consequently the oracle stands here as a memorial of the truthfulness of the prophecy; and it answers a further purpose still, viz., to furnish a rich prophetic consolation for the church of all times, when persecuted by the world, and sighing under the oppression of the kingdom of the world.  <chapter eID="Isa.16"/> <div eID="gen13029" type="x-p"/>

entries.4d927ef2185ee572cb2319d564c645bc1f6e0859: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.1" sID="gen42861" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42862" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Send ye a lamb.</hi> Here the Prophet scoffs at the Moabites for not acknowledging God at the proper time, but recklessly waiting for the stroke of his hand, till they were completely destroyed. It is, therefore, a condemnation of late repentance, when men cannot be brought to obedience by any warnings, and continue in obstinate opposition to God. Where the disease is incurable, an exhortation of this kind is appropriate; and this ought to be carefully observed, for both Jews and Christians misinterpret this passage.<div eID="gen42862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42863" type="x-p"/>Jerome explains it as referring to Christ, because he drew his birth from the Moabites, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ruth.1.4">Ruth 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.5">Matthew 1:5</reference>,) from whom Ruth was descended; and that opinion has been adopted by almost all Christians; as if the Prophet had said, “O Lord, though a judgment so severe as this awaits the Moabites, still thou wilt not utterly destroy them; for they will send thee <hi type="italic">a Lamb, the ruler of the world.”</hi> But that interpretation, being destitute of plausibility, need not be refuted.<div eID="gen42863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42864" type="x-p"/>On the other hand, the Jews think that these words were spoken because, while the Jews were in a depressed condition, the Moabites ceased to pay the tribute which they owed them, but that, after having prophesied about the restoration of the kingdom of Judah, Isaiah likewise added an exhortation to remind them to acknowledge their king. They even go so far as to say that it serves the purpose of a royal edict, taking them to task for their disloyalty, “Send the tribute which you owe.” But we nowhere read that the Moabites were subjects or tributaries to the Jews, and there is no probability in the conjecture. Nor does the passage which they quote (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.3.5 Bible:2Kgs.3.6">2 Kings 3:5, 6</reference>) give them any support; for that passage relates to <hi type="italic">the king of Israel</hi>, and expressly mentions <hi type="italic">Ahab</hi> and <hi type="italic">Samaria</hi>, who cherished, as we are aware, the utmost hatred against the Jews.<div eID="gen42864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42865" type="x-p"/>I therefore adhere to the interpretation which I first noticed, as the true and natural interpretation; for the design of the Prophet is to condemn the Moabites for not having repented in due season, and to tell them that they will now in vain do what they might easily have done formerly, and with great advantage to themselves. We ought, therefore, to view it as spoken ironically, (<foreign xml:lang="el">εἰρωνικῶς</foreign>,) <hi type="italic">Send</hi>; as if he had said that there is no hope of pardon, that they will <hi type="italic">send</hi> in vain. When the wicked are warned, they indolently disregard all exhortation; when they are punished, they gaze around them with distressful looks, seeking assistance in every direction, and trying every method of relief, but unsuccessfully, for they gain no advantage. Isaiah, therefore, reproaches them for obstinacy and rebellion, and shows that there will be no time for repentance, when they meet with the destruction which they deserve.<div eID="gen42865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42866" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To the ruler of the world.</hi> The opinion of the Jews, that this denotes Hezekiah, is at variance with all reason; for <foreign xml:lang="he">ארץ</foreign> (<hi type="italic">eretz</hi>) does not here denote a particular country, but rather the whole <hi type="italic">world</hi>, of which he speaks in general terms. The appellation <hi type="italic">Ruler</hi> must therefore be viewed as referring to God himself. By <hi type="italic">a</hi> <hi type="italic">lamb</hi>, he means what was to be offered in sacrifice; for even the Gentiles acknowledged that they worshipped God when they offered sacrifices.<div eID="gen42866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42867" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">From the rock</hi> <note n="249"> <div sID="gen42868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">From Sela</hi>, (or, <hi type="italic">Petra</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42869" type="x-p"/> FT241 “Petra, <hi type="italic">Rock</hi>, also called Sela, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.16.1">Isaiah 16:1</reference>,) and Joktheel, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Kgs.14.7">2 Kings 14:7</reference>.) The capital of Idumea, and one of the most remarkable cities of the ancient world. For more than a thousand years this city remained unknown and unvisited, till Burckhardt discovered it in 1812. It was afterwards visited, with some difficulty, by Messrs. Legh, Banks, Captains Irby and Mangles, as well as by M. Linant and M. Laborde.” Those who have not access to the details of those enterprizing researches, or who wish to see it ably stated and argued, that “the present condition of <hi type="italic">Petra</hi> furnishes a remarkable fulfillment of Scripture prophecy,” will do well to read the article Petra in Dr. Eadie’s <hi type="italic">Biblical</hi> <hi type="italic">Cyclopaedia</hi>, from which the above extracts are taken; an article which draws largely both from the narratives of travelers and from the inspired writers, and compresses within moderate limits a large amount of information. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen42869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42870" type="x-p"/> FT242 <hi type="italic">As a wandering bird</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42871" type="x-p"/> FT243 <hi type="italic">Take</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">Bring</hi>) <hi type="italic">counsel</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42872" type="x-p"/> FT244 “Make a shadow for thee <hi type="italic">at noon</hi>, to throw darkness over thee, <hi type="italic">as in the night</hi>, that by means of it thou mayest be concealed from the face of thy enemies.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi><div eID="gen42872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42873" type="x-p"/> FT245 <hi type="italic">For the extortioner</hi> (Heb. <hi type="italic">wringer</hi>) <hi type="italic">is at an end</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42874" type="x-p"/> FT246 <hi type="italic">Until the extortioner</hi> <foreign xml:lang="he">כי</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ki</hi>) answers here to the Latin adverb, <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">usquedum</hi></foreign>. — <hi type="italic">Tayl. Concord</hi>. quoted by Stock.<div eID="gen42874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42875" type="x-p"/> FT247 <hi type="italic">And in mercy shall the throne be established</hi>,(or, <hi type="italic">prepared</hi>.) — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42876" type="x-p"/> FT248 <hi type="italic">His wrath</hi>. — Eng. Ver. In the author’s version of this chapter, the rendering is, <hi type="italic">his insolence</hi>; but in his margin he puts <hi type="italic">indignation</hi>. Lowth and Stock make it <hi type="italic">his anger</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen42876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42877" type="x-p"/> FT249 The rendering of the Septuagint is, <foreign xml:lang="el">οὐχ οὕτως ἡ μαντεία σου</foreign>,<foreign xml:lang="el"> οὐχ οὕτως</foreign> <hi type="italic">Not so thy divination, not so</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen42877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42878" type="x-p"/> FT250 <foreign xml:lang="he">לא כן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">lo ken</hi>,) <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">non rectum</hi></foreign>, the frivolous predictions of his diviners, on which no wise man would place dependence. — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi><div eID="gen42878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42879" type="x-p"/> FT251 <hi type="italic">Therefore shall Moab howl for Moab</hi>. — Eng. Ver. <hi type="italic">Moan even ye who</hi> yourselves <hi type="italic">are smitten</hi>. — <hi type="italic">Stock</hi><div eID="gen42880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42881" type="x-p"/> FT253 <hi type="italic">For the fields of Heshbon languish</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42882" type="x-p"/> FT254 “It ought to be known that Heshbon was a place of <hi type="italic">fields</hi>, and Sibmah was a place of vineyards. If you object, that all these cities were on the other side of Jordan, and at what time therefore did they fall under the hand (or power) of the Moabites? we reply. When Sennacherib carried the Reubenites and Gadites into captivity, the Moabites, who were their neighbors, came and dwelt in those cities.” — <hi type="italic">Jarchi</hi><div eID="gen42882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42883" type="x-p"/> FT255 <hi type="italic">The lords of the heathen have trodden down the principal plants</hi> <hi type="italic">thereof</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42884" type="x-p"/> FT256 <hi type="italic">They are come even unto Jazer</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42885" type="x-p"/> FT257 “<hi type="italic">The lake of Jazer</hi>, as Jeremiah explains it, <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.32">Jeremiah 48:32</reference>. The plantations of this vine spread onward to the banks, and seemed to overhang the whole breadth of the lake.” — <hi type="italic">Rosenmuller</hi><div eID="gen42885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42886" type="x-p"/> FT258 <hi type="italic">For the shouting for thy summer-fruits and for thy harvest is</hi> <hi type="italic">fallen</hi>. Georg</hi>. 2:417.<div eID="gen42887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42888" type="x-p"/> FT260 <hi type="italic">But he shall not prevail</hi>. — Eng. Ver.<div eID="gen42888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42889" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen42889" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic"> of the desert.</hi> He gives the name of <hi type="italic">the rock of the desert</hi> to the city, which is supposed to have been the chief city of the Moabites; <note n="250"> <div sID="gen42890" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42890" type="x-p"/> </note> though it is possible that he intended to include the whole of the country, and thus a part will be taken for the whole.<div eID="gen42867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42891" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To the mountain of the daughter of Zion;</hi> that is, to God’s authorized temple, in which sacrifices were offered according to the injunction of the Law. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.12.5 Bible:Deut.12.6 Bible:Deut.12.7">Deuteronomy 12:5, 6, 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:2Chr.7.12">2 Chronicles 7:12</reference>.) This is a remarkable passage against obstinate men, who set aside all instruction, and fearlessly despise God, till they are visited by his judgments.<div eID="gen42891" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42861" osisID="Isa.16.1" type="section"/>
entries.6e90d4db34f4f22db2da982c4d8b07c6ec1feb37: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.2" sID="gen42892" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi><hi type="italic"> It shall be as a bird let loose.</hi> <note n="251"> <div sID="gen42894" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42894" type="x-p"/> </note> The Prophet now shows what he meant by the former mockery, that the Moabites ought not at that time to think of <hi type="italic">sending</hi> sacrifices, because they will not be able to provide for their safety in any other way than by leaving their native country. By the metaphor of <hi type="italic">birds</hi> he describes the terror with which they shall be struck, so that they will flee even at the rustling of a leaf. He threatens that the Moabites, who had abused their tranquillity, shall have a trembling and wearisome flight.<div eID="gen42893" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42892" osisID="Isa.16.2" type="section"/>
entries.3a9eb7ab45c07c4107235f4b5c3574fbd51304d7: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.3" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.3" sID="gen42895" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> <hi type="italic">Assemble a council.</hi> <note n="252"> <div sID="gen42897" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42897" type="x-p"/> </note> He proceeds with the same subject; for if we wish rightly to understand this passage, we must set before our minds the dreadful ruin of the Moabites. Their crimes are brought to remembrance, that all may see more clearly how deservedly they are punished. When everything was in their power, they freely indulged in licentiousness, and would not listen to any reproofs; but now, when they are deprived of everything, they groan, and seek remedies which are nowhere to be found. The Lord deals with the reprobate in such a manner that, in order to leave them without excuse, he bestows upon them, and places in their hands, everything that they need; but when, through their wicked passion, they have abused and turned everything to a wicked purpose, he deprives them of all aid and support, and utterly destroys them.<div eID="gen42896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42898" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Execute judgment.</hi> While the Moabites enjoyed prosperity, they cared little about what was good and right; while it was in their power to rule, and to have their kingdom established, in a just manner, they abused their power for the purpose of tyranny. Now that they were stripped of all authority, and were exiles and fugitives, Isaiah ironically advises them to <hi type="italic">assemble councils</hi> and <hi type="italic">execute</hi> <hi type="italic">judgments</hi>, which they had formerly overturned through fraud and injustice. Isaiah has in view that time when all power and authority was taken out of the hands of the Moabites. The upbraiding is similar to that with which the Lord addresses Adam, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.3.22">Genesis 3:22</reference>,) <hi type="italic">Behold, Adam</hi> <hi type="italic">is become as one of us</hi>, ridiculing him with the biting taunt, that he was not satisfied with his exalted attainments, and wished to rival God himself.<div eID="gen42898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42899" type="x-p"/>In like manner, the Moabites, not satisfied with their ornaments and wealth, wretchedly harassed and plundered the Israelites and Jews, and formed wicked plans against them. Having abused the excellent gift of God, they therefore deserved to have this reproof addressed to them, which is equally applicable to all the reprobate, who proudly vaunt in prosperity and barbarously abuse it for harassing the godly. Seeing that they basely pollute those things which the Lord had set apart to their proper use, it is right that they should be deprived of them and reduced to the lowest poverty. We have instances of this every day. How comes it that those who were raised to the highest rank of honor fall down headlong, but because the Lord punishes their tyrannical rule and their crimes? The Lord also ridicules their upbraiding and reproachful language, their wailings, and even their complaints; as when they exclaim, “O that I had the wealth which I once enjoyed! O that I were restored to my former condition!” For then repentance will be too late.<div eID="gen42899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42900" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Make thy shadow.</hi> The Moabites might, as I have already hinted, have given some relief to the wretched Jews, when they were harassed by the Assyrians; or, at least, if they had had a spark of humanity, they ought to have protected the fugitives; but, on the contrary, they persecuted them, and added to the weight of their afflictions, which were already oppressive. It was highly proper that the Moabites should be the subjects of that cruelty which they had exercised towards others; that, when they had been driven from their dwellings, and were exiles and wanderers, they should nowhere find any solace, any <hi type="italic">shadow</hi> to shelter them from the heat; for why should they enjoy the consolations which they had barbarously refused to others?<div eID="gen42900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42901" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">As the night in the midst of noon-day.</hi> <note n="253"> <div sID="gen42902" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42902" type="x-p"/> </note> By <hi type="italic">noon-day</hi> is here meant the most scorching heat. This metaphor is frequently employed in Scripture, that the Lord was <hi type="italic">like a cloud at noon, and like a pillar</hi> <hi type="italic">of fire by night</hi>; for he once was so in the wilderness. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Exod.13.21 Bible:Exod.13.22">Exodus 13:21, 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Num.14.14">Numbers 14:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.1.33">Deuteronomy 1:33</reference>.) This mode of expression, being customary, was retained by the Prophets, though they did not relate the history.<div eID="gen42901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42903" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Hide the banished.</hi> He means the Jews, whom the Assyrians persecuted and harassed, and whom the Moabites at the same time treated cruelly. It was their duty to shelter and relieve the fugitives, and especially those who fled to them for protection; but seeing that they drove them out, it was proper that they should be driven out in the same manner, and deprived of all assistance and support; for it is a righteous sentence which the Lord pronounces, when he enjoins that <hi type="italic">the same measure</hi> <hi type="italic">which every one metes shall be measured to him again</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.19.19 Bible:Deut.19.21">Deuteronomy 19:19, 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.7.2">Matthew 7:2</reference>.) Now the Prophet calls on the Moabites to acknowledge their sins, so as to confess that they are justly punished for their cruelty. Yet he rather has the Jews in his eye, in order to inform them that God does not disregard their afflictions, for they are told that he will be their avenger.<div eID="gen42903" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.3" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42895" osisID="Isa.16.3" type="section"/>
entries.2e16cdb427b3283a97add5f13914a59e64dbf7ea: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.4" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.4" sID="gen42904" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> <hi type="italic">Let mine outcasts dwell with thee, Moab.</hi> The Prophet addresses the <hi type="italic">Moabites</hi>, as if he were humbly beseeching them in the name of the people at large. “You are neighbors, related to us by blood; receive and assist those who are in distress: and if you do not choose to assist, at least do them no harm.” God, who usually undertakes the cause of his people, is represented by the Prophet as if he performed the part of a suppliant. It is certain, that the Moabites did not at all act in this manner towards the Jews, but, on the contrary, that they joined their efforts with the enemies of the Jews to do them injury. But, as I said a little before, the Prophet sets before our eyes that justice which even nature demands, that the cruel violation of it may be the more abhorred.<div eID="gen42905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42906" type="x-p"/>This passage ought to be carefully observed; for God shows how great is the care which he takes of his people, since the injuries done to them affect him in the same manner as if they had been done to himself; as he declares by Zechariah, that <hi type="italic">whenever they are touched, the apple of</hi> <hi type="italic">his eye is touched</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Zech.2.8">Zechariah 2:8</reference>.) He <hi type="italic">hears the groaning</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.102.20">Psalm 102:20</reference>,) and observes the tears, of wretched men who call upon him; (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.12.5 Bible:Ps.38.9">Psalm 12:5, 38:9</reference>;) and though this be not always visible to us, yet in due season he shows that he has heard them.<div eID="gen42906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42907" type="x-p"/>Let us therefore learn from this passage to be kind and dutiful to fugitives and exiles, and especially to believers, who are banished for their confession of the word. No duty can be more pleasing or acceptable to God; and, on the other hand, nothing is more hateful or abominable in his sight than barbarity and cruelty. If we wish to obtain any alleviation of our calamities, let us be kind and compassionate, and not refuse assistance to the needy.<div eID="gen42907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42908" type="x-p"/>Blessed, says he, is he that judgeth wisely about the poor and needy; the Lord will deliver him in the evil day.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.41.1">Psalm 41:1</reference>.)<div eID="gen42908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42909" type="x-p"/>On the other hand,<div eID="gen42909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42910" type="x-p"/>he shall have judgment without mercy who hath showed no mercy. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.2.13">James 2:13</reference>.)<div eID="gen42910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42911" type="x-p"/>When God calls them <hi type="italic">his banished</hi>, this may without impropriety be viewed as referring to punishment, as if he said, that by a just judgment they were <hi type="italic">banished</hi> from the land of Canaan, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.28.64">Deuteronomy 28:64</reference>,) as he had so often threatened against them. Yet undoubtedly he likewise means, that they continue to be under his defense and protection, because, though they are banished and driven out of their native country, still he acknowledges them to be his people. That calamity which the Jews endured might be regarded as an evidence that they were cast off; but the Lord acknowledges them to be <hi type="italic">his children</hi>, though he chastises them severely. Hence we obtain a doctrine full of consolation, that we are reckoned in the number of his children, though sharp and heavy strokes are inflicted upon us.<div eID="gen42911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42912" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">For the extortioner hath ceased.</hi> <note n="254"> <div sID="gen42913" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42913" type="x-p"/> </note> He now directs his discourse to the Jews, and proceeds to comfort them, as he had done formerly, by showing that, when their enemies shall be removed from the midst of them, the banishment or ruin of their enemies will also relieve their own calamities and distresses. Yet the former statements related chiefly to the Jews, though the Prophet expressly addressed the Moabites. But at that time he only threatened vengeance on enemies, while here he more clearly promises consolation to his people; as if he had said, “Thou thoughtest, O Moab, that my people were utterly ruined: but I will restrain the enemies, and put an end to that affliction. Thou shalt therefore perish; but my people shall at length be delivered from those dreadful calamities.”<div eID="gen42912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42914" type="x-p"/>Perhaps it will rather be thought that there is a change of the tenses; and thus the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">כי</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">ki</hi>,) which we have rendered <hi type="italic">For</hi>, will signify <hi type="italic">Until</hi>; <note n="255"> <div sID="gen42915" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42915" type="x-p"/> </note> and this clause will be read in immediate connection with the former part of the sentence. <hi type="italic">Let my banished dwell with thee, Moab; be thou a place of concealment from the face of the destroyer, until the extortioner shall have ceased</hi>. But as that might be thought to be a forced interpretation, I have chosen to abide by the natural meaning.<div eID="gen42914" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.4" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42904" osisID="Isa.16.4" type="section"/>
entries.4e2970f0497a5c388bcc895df868592571aecc30: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.5" sID="gen42916" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And the throne shall be prepared in mercy.</hi> <note n="256"> <div sID="gen42918" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42918" type="x-p"/> </note> The Jews explain the whole of this verse as referring to Hezekiah; but this is altogether inappropriate, for the Prophet speaks of a more important restoration of the Church, and the Moabites had not been punished during the flourishing condition of Hezekiah’s reign; and the blessing of God again began to burst forth on the Jews. It is as if it had been said “All the enemies of the chosen people maliciously contrive the ruin of that kingdom, which God promised <hi type="italic">should be established for ever</hi>.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.13">2 Samuel 7:13</reference>.) That the godly may not give way to despondency amidst the unhappy confusion, they are reminded of the perpetuity of the kingdom, of which they had been assured by a well-known prediction.<div eID="gen42917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42919" type="x-p"/>It cannot therefore be explained as referring to any other than to Christ, though I acknowledge that Hezekiah was a type of Christ, as David and the rest of his successors also were. But they conduct us to Christ, who alone is the protector and leader of his people, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.10.16">John 10:16</reference>,) and who has <hi type="italic">gathered the remnant that was scattered abroad</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.11.52">John 11:52</reference>.) For this reason he sends back the godly to Christ, as if he had said, “You know what God you worship. He has declared that he will watch over your safety, so that under his protection you will always continue to be safe and uninjured; and if you shall at any time meet with reverses, he has promised to you a Redeemer, under whom you shall enjoy renewed and steadfast prosperity. Though for a time you may weep, yet the protector of the Church will come, and will restore you to a flourishing state of freedom. You ought, therefore, with your whole heart, to rely on the expectation of him; even when you see the Church to be in a confused and wretched condition.”<div eID="gen42919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42920" type="x-p"/>This ought to be carefully observed; for all other consolations are transitory and fading, if we do not refer all of them to Christ. Let our eyes therefore be fixed on him, if we wish to be happy and prosperous; for he has promised that we shall be happy even amidst the cross, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.5.10 Bible:Matt.5.11">Matthew 5:10,11</reference>,) that agony and torments will open up the way to a blessed life, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.17">2 Corinthians 4:17</reference>,) and that all the afflictions which we shall suffer will add to the amount of our happiness. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.8.28">Romans 8:28</reference>.)<div eID="gen42920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42921" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In mercy.</hi> Isaiah shows that this does not take place through the agency of men, but by the kindness of God, who is the builder of this <hi type="italic">throne</hi>; and therefore we ought to acknowledge that it is owing to his undeserved goodness that this sacred <hi type="italic">throne</hi> is established among us. The Prophet expressly confirms this by saying, that the cause of it must not be sought anywhere else than in the absolute <hi type="italic">mercy</hi> of God. Nor can any other cause be found; for God could not be induced by any excellence of character, or by merits, (of which there certainly were none,) to set up again the throne which had fallen down through the fault and through the crimes of the people; but when he saw that those whom he had adopted were ruined, he wished to give a proof of his infinite goodness. Now, if God build this throne, by whom shall it be overturned? Will wicked men be stronger than he?<div eID="gen42921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42922" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And he will sit upon it in the tabernacle of David.</hi> Almost every word here is emphatic, so that this verse deserves to be continually pondered. I do not object to the opinion that the word <hi type="italic">tabernacle</hi> contains an allusion to this effect, that he was but an ordinary man before he was <hi type="italic">called to sit on a throne</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Sam.16.11 Bible:1Sam.16.12">1 Samuel 16:11, 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:2Sam.7.8">2 Samuel 7:8</reference>.) The Prophet intended to draw a picture of the Church, which has no resemblance to the thrones of kings and of princes, and does not shine with gold or precious stones. Though he has held out the spiritual kingdom of Christ under a mean and despicable shape, yet at the same time he shows that that kingdom will be seen on earth and amongst men. If he had only said that <hi type="italic">the throne</hi> of Christ will be erected, we might have asked, Will his <hi type="italic">throne</hi> be in heaven, or also on earth? But now when he says, <hi type="italic">in the tabernacle of David</hi>, he shows that Christ reigns not only among angels but also among men, lest we should think that, in order to seek him, we must enter into heaven. Wicked men ridicule what we preach about the kingdom of Christ, as if it were some phantom of our own imagination. They wish to see it with their eyes, and to have the evidence of their senses; but we ought not to conceive of it as at all carnal, but to be satisfied with his arm and with his power.<div eID="gen42922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42923" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">In steadfastness. </hi><foreign xml:lang="he">אמת</foreign> (<hi type="italic">emeth</hi>) denotes not only <hi type="italic">truth</hi> but every kind of <hi type="italic">certainty</hi>. The Prophet means that the kingdom of Christ will be firm and steadfast, as Daniel also declared. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.2.44 Bible:Dan.7.14">Daniel 2:44, 7:14</reference>.) The Evangelist also says, <hi type="italic">Of his kingdom there</hi> <hi type="italic">shall be no end</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.33">Luke 1:33</reference>.) In this respect it is distinguished from the ordinary condition of kingdoms, which, even when they are founded on great and enormous wealth, crumble down or even fall by their own weight, so that they have no more permanency than vanishing pictures. But Isaiah declares, that the kingdom of Christ, though it frequently totter, will be supported by the hand of God, and therefore will last for ever. These proofs ought to fortify us against temptations which arise, whenever the kingdom of Christ is attacked by enemies so numerous and powerful that we might be ready to think that it will quickly be destroyed. Whatever weapons the world may employ, and though hell itself should vomit out flames of fire, we must abide by this promise.<div eID="gen42923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42924" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Who shall judge.</hi> I understand <foreign xml:lang="he">שפת</foreign> (<hi type="italic">shophet</hi>) to mean <hi type="italic">Governor</hi>, as if he had said, “There will be one who shall <hi type="italic">govern</hi>.” Often do we see a magnificent throne when there is no one to sit on it, and it frequently happens that kings are either idols or cattle, without judgment or skill or wisdom. But here he says, that one will sit who shall discharge the office of a good <hi type="italic">governor</hi>; and this is added in order to assure us that Christ will be our protector.<div eID="gen42924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42925" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And seek judgment and hasten righteousness.</hi> The <hi type="italic">judgment</hi> and the <hi type="italic">righteousness</hi> which are ascribed to him, are nothing else than the protection under which he receives us, and which he will not allow to be infringed; for he will not allow wicked men who injure us to pass unpunished, while we patiently and calmly commit ourselves to his protection. By the word <hi type="italic">hasten</hi> he shows that he will quickly and speedily avenge our cause. This must be viewed as a rebuke to our impatience, for we never think that his assistance comes soon enough. But when we are hurried along by the violence of passion, let us remember that this arises from not submitting to his providence; for although according to the judgment of our flesh he delays, still he regulates his judgment in the best manner by the seasons which are well known to him. Let us therefore submit to his will.<div eID="gen42925" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42916" osisID="Isa.16.5" type="section"/>
entries.1453049d965aeb950846bc3c90acf3806fc6c0a3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.6" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.6" sID="gen42926" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42927" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> <hi type="italic">We have heard of the pride of Moab.</hi> The Prophet added this statement by way of anticipation. It might be thought that men could not believe what he had promised about restoring the <hi type="italic">throne</hi> of the king and destroying the Moabites, who at that time were in a flourishing state of riches, and were defended by strong fortresses, and who, puffed up with the prosperity which they now enjoyed, were exceedingly <hi type="italic">proud</hi>. Besides, their haughtiness, with which they scorned the unhappy Jews, was a disagreeable and powerful weapon for discouraging or shaking their minds. To provide against this temptation, he relates that their boasting was well known, but that their <hi type="italic">pride</hi> would not prevent God from overthrowing them; because no array of armed forces, no treasures of riches, no multitude of men, can withstand God. Isaiah speaks of it as a thing extensively known, that the Moabites are puffed up in such a manner that they dread nothing; as is commonly the case with those who are well supplied with riches and troops, that they idly exalt themselves above God and men. But whatever may be their arrogance, the Lord will easily restrain it.<div eID="gen42927" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42928" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">His insolence.</hi> <note n="257"> <div sID="gen42929" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42929" type="x-p"/> </note> The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">עברה</foreign> (<hi type="italic">gnebrah</hi>) most frequently signifies <hi type="italic">indignation</hi>; but the connection in which it stands appears to call for something more definite. This noun is derived from the verb <foreign xml:lang="he">עבר</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">gnabar</hi>,) to <hi type="italic">pass</hi> or <hi type="italic">go beyond</hi>, answering to the Latin word <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">excessus</hi></foreign>; and therefore I have thought it better to translate it <hi type="italic">insolence</hi>. In a parallel passage, after the words <hi type="italic">pride</hi> and <hi type="italic">arrogance</hi> comes the phrase <hi type="italic">haughtiness of</hi> <hi type="italic">heart</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.29">Jeremiah 48:29</reference>.) Both Isaiah and Jeremiah, I have no doubt, mean that the Moabites, in consequence of their stubborn and disdainful behavior, and their sumptuous mode of living, were so cruel, that they kindled into wrath on the most trivial occasions, and rose fiercely against others. This vice is always accompanied by haughtiness of mind; for <hi type="italic">pride</hi> is followed by disdain and contempt of others, and they who claim more than is due to them easily kindle into rage, and become furious for the smallest offense. In short, they can bear nothing, and are not only passionate, but likewise outrageous. They would wish that all should yield to them, and that they should yield to none. If all do not yield at their bidding, they think that injustice is done to them. This passionate temper is easily betrayed by proud men. On the other hand, the humble possess kindness accompanied by corresponding modesty, and easily forgive any one who has injured them.<div eID="gen42928" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42930" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">His lies.</hi> The Hebrew word <foreign xml:lang="he">בדים</foreign> (<hi type="italic">baddim</hi>) denotes either <hi type="italic">a mans limbs</hi>, or <hi type="italic">the branches of a tree</hi>, and sometimes it is put for <hi type="italic">divination</hi>. Accordingly, the Greek translators <note n="258"> <div sID="gen42931" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42931" type="x-p"/> </note> render it <foreign xml:lang="el">μαντεἰα</foreign>, <hi type="italic">divination</hi>, and it has that signification in other passages. Some think that it is here used metaphorically for <hi type="italic">children</hi>; others translate it either <hi type="italic">discourses</hi> or <hi type="italic">thoughts</hi>; and others render it <hi type="italic">strength</hi> or <hi type="italic">sinews</hi>. But in my opinion it is rather put for <hi type="italic">vain boasting</hi>; for this word often denotes <hi type="italic">falsehood</hi>, and we shall soon see how well this signification applies to the present passage.<div eID="gen42930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42932" type="x-p"/>There is quite as much difference in the interpretation of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">כן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ken</hi>,) <hi type="italic">so</hi>. The greater part suppose it to mean that “the lies are not right,” or that “the discourses are not right,” and others, that “the lies are not true;” and as to the substance of the matter, I am almost of their opinion. I have no doubt that the meaning of the Prophet is, that Moab foolishly utters his vain boastings, for he will not accomplish what he imagines. As to the words, the meaning of them is obtained with greater certainty from <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.30">Jeremiah 48:30</reference>. After the same words which are here employed by Isaiah, he immediately adds, for the sake of explaining them, <foreign xml:lang="he">לא כן</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">lo ken</hi>,) <hi type="italic">Not so</hi>; <note n="259"> <div sID="gen42933" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42933" type="x-p"/> </note> <hi type="italic">his lies shall not so effect it.</hi> As if he had said, “What is determined in their hearts shall fail of accomplishment.” Yet I do not think, that in the former clause the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">כן</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ken</hi>) denotes comparison, but rather confirmation, so to speak, but negatively; for he declares that there will be no firmness or stability in his counsels, that <hi type="italic">his</hi> <hi type="italic">divinations</hi> or <hi type="italic">lies will not take effect</hi>. Proud men settle everything as if everything were in their power, and were not subject to the providence of God. “Such <hi type="italic">arrogance</hi>,” says Isaiah, shall be brought down, and all that they promise, as to their own strength, shall vanish away. This reminds us that pride is highly displeasing to God, and that the more men are puffed up with their riches, they are the nearer to destruction.<div eID="gen42932" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.6" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42926" osisID="Isa.16.6" type="section"/>
entries.7634e46bad43f75c1d221af101d73ec2670ebb2c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.7" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.7" sID="gen42934" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi><hi type="italic"> Therefore shall Moab howl to Moab.</hi> <note n="260"> <div sID="gen42936" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42936" type="x-p"/> </note> He declares more plainly what has been already said, that this <hi type="italic">pride</hi>, and the cruelty which springs from it, will be the cause of their destruction. Since the Lord <hi type="italic">resisteth the proud</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jas.4.6">James 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.5">1 Peter 5:5</reference>,) it is impossible but that he will lay low this haughtiness, by which the Church is basely and shamefully trampled under foot; and, according to this example, the end of all proud men must be mournful. When he adds, <hi type="italic">Moab to Moab</hi>, he means that there will be what may be called a melancholy concert among them, in which they shall mutually complain of their calamities and bewail their distresses among themselves. Others render it, <hi type="italic">on</hi> <hi type="italic">account of Moab</hi>, but this is a feeble interpretation; for immediately afterwards it follows that the <hi type="italic">howling</hi> will be universal, or that it will be throughout the whole of the people.<div eID="gen42935" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42937" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">On account of the foundations of Kir-hareseth.</hi> It is sufficiently evident that this was a chief and royal city; but some consider it to be a proper name, and others to be an appellative. There can be no doubt that the etymology of the word was derived from its being constructed of earthen materials. It is also possible that it received this name on account of the nature of the walls, which were built of bricks. It was a distinguished city in that country. He names <hi type="italic">the foundations</hi> rather than the city itself, because it was to be completely thrown down; as if he had said, “You shall not mourn the plundering of the city or the destruction of the buildings, but its entire overthrow; for no part of it shall be left.”<div eID="gen42937" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42938" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">You will groan, being only smitten.</hi> <note n="261"> <div sID="gen42939" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42939" type="x-p"/> </note> Some translate <foreign xml:lang="he">נכאים</foreign> (<hi type="italic">nechaim</hi>) <hi type="italic">lame</hi>; but I prefer to take it as meaning <hi type="italic">smitten</hi>. The particle <foreign xml:lang="he">אך</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">ach</hi>,) which is here prefixed to it, sometimes means <hi type="italic">certainly</hi> or <hi type="italic">truly</hi>; and sometimes it is put for <hi type="italic">but</hi> or <hi type="italic">notwithstanding</hi>. Those who explain it affirmatively suppose the meaning to be this, <hi type="italic">You will groan, being truly smitten</hi>; that is, “It will not be necessary for you to hire men to pretend mourning in your name, as is usually done in funerals, but you will mourn in earnest.” But I prefer to take <foreign xml:lang="he">אך</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ach</hi>) as meaning <hi type="italic">only</hi>; that is, “All who shall be left will be wounded; not one shall be safe.” By this mode of expression he describes the utter destruction of that city, and intimates that those who are left will lament not only the distresses of others, but also their own. They, too, will be wounded. And if such severe punishments are inflicted on the <hi type="italic">proud</hi>, let us learn to submit ourselves with humility and modesty, and willingly to <hi type="italic">humble</hi> <hi type="italic">ourselves under the mighty hand of God</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.5.6">1 Peter 5:6</reference>.)<div eID="gen42938" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42934" osisID="Isa.16.7" type="section"/>
entries.6546ba47d2f130652fa22e6ec9de7580b9d389c8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.8" sID="gen42940" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42941" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8. </hi><hi type="italic">For the vines of Heshbon have been cut down.</hi> <note n="262"> <div sID="gen42942" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42942" type="x-p"/> </note> Here the Prophet describes allegorically the desolation of the whole country. There is reason to believe that it abounded in the choicest <hi type="italic">vines</hi>, <note n="263"> <div sID="gen42943" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42943" type="x-p"/> </note> as may readily be inferred from this and the parallel passage. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.32">Jeremiah 48:32</reference>.) When Prophets threaten destruction to countries, they usually delineate their more remarkable features. For instance, were we to speak of Picardy, we certainly would say nothing about <hi type="italic">vines</hi>, as if we had been speaking about Orleans or Burgundy. Now, the cities mentioned by the Prophet were the chief cities of Moab.<div eID="gen42941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42944" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The lords of the nations have trodden down his choicest shoots</hi> or <hi type="italic">branches.</hi> <note n="264"> <div sID="gen42945" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42945" type="x-p"/> </note> The Prophet says that <hi type="italic">the most valuable branches</hi> of their vineyards were torn out by <hi type="italic">the lords of the nations</hi>, that is, by the conquerors, who, having subdued the nations in war, held extensive dominion.<div eID="gen42944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42946" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Which reached even to Jazer.</hi> <note n="265"> <div sID="gen42947" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42947" type="x-p"/> </note> This serves to point out the extent of the devastation; for this city was situated on the confines of the land of the Moabites; as if he had said, “Not only shall a part of the vineyards be cut down, but the whole country shall be wasted far and wide.” Some refer this to the enemies themselves; but I would rather supply the relative <foreign xml:lang="he">אשר</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">asher</hi>,) <hi type="italic">which</hi>, and refer it to <hi type="italic">the vines, which</hi> were so extensive that they <hi type="italic">reached even to Jazer</hi>. Thus the meaning will be, “Though these vineyards <hi type="italic">reached even to Jazer</hi>, and covered a very large tract of country, yet thence <hi type="italic">to the wilderness</hi> they will all be trodden down by <hi type="italic">the lords of</hi> <hi type="italic">the nations</hi>.” This agrees best with the scope of the passage; for it is immediately added that the vineyards <hi type="italic">reached to the wilderness</hi>, and even <hi type="italic">to the sea</hi>; by which he means that the country was exceedingly fertile, and especially that it abounded in <hi type="italic">vines</hi>. He says that they <hi type="italic">crossed the sea</hi>, <note n="266"> <div sID="gen42948" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42948" type="x-p"/> </note> because, when the soil is productive, it is customary to protect by mounds what is contiguous to the sea, in order to extend the cultivation, and to oppose the violence of the waves by posts of wood and embankments, in order to obtain a large extent of available soil.<div eID="gen42946" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42940" osisID="Isa.16.8" type="section"/>
entries.09428b9efb978674ef035f257ff672efc7fc35ef: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.9" sID="gen42949" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">Therefore I will bewail.</hi> The Prophet here takes upon him the character of another person, as we have formerly remarked; for in the name of the Moabites he laments and groans. It is undoubtedly true that believers always shudder at the judgments of God, and cannot lay aside the feelings of human nature, so as not to commiserate the destruction of the wicked. Yet he does not describe his own feelings; but his intention is to give additional weight to his instruction, that no one may entertain a doubt as to the accomplishment. He therefore represents in the person of a Moabite, as on a stage, the mourning and grief which shall be felt by all after that calamity, in order to hold out to the Jews a confirmation of this promise, which otherwise might have been thought to be incredible.<div eID="gen42950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42951" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Because on thy summer-fruits and on thy harvest a shouting shall break forth,</hi> or <hi type="italic">shall fall.</hi> <note n="267"> <div sID="gen42952" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42952" type="x-p"/> </note> This last clause of the verse is variously explained by commentators. <foreign xml:lang="he">נפל</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">naphal</hi>,) signifies to <hi type="italic">fall</hi>, or to <hi type="italic">burst forth</hi>. Those who translate it, <hi type="italic">to burst</hi> <hi type="italic">forth</hi>, consider the word <foreign xml:lang="he">הידד</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">hedad</hi>,) <hi type="italic">shouting</hi>, to refer to the enemies themselves; as if he had said, “<hi type="italic">The shouting</hi> of enemies <hi type="italic">bursts forth on thy harvest;”</hi> so that there is an implied contrast between this <hi type="italic">shouting</hi> and the <hi type="italic">joy</hi> of which he will afterwards speak. Others explain it to mean, that <hi type="italic">the shoutings will be laid;</hi> that is, “there shall be no more <hi type="italic">shouting</hi>, and no longer shall the glad and merry voices of the reapers be heard, cheering themselves after the harvest.” But I would rather refer it to the <hi type="italic">shouting</hi> of enemies; and on this point I follow a most faithful interpreter of this passage, the Prophet Jeremiah, who says that <hi type="italic">the</hi> <hi type="italic">spoiler bursts forth</hi>, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.48.32">Jeremiah 48:32</reference>,) where Isaiah speaks of the <hi type="italic">shouting</hi> of the enemy; as if he had said, “When thou shalt make preparations for gathering in thy harvest and thy vintage, the enemies will <hi type="italic">rush</hi> in, and, instead of joy and cheerful song, their <hi type="italic">shouting</hi> shall be heard, which shall drive thee far away.”<div eID="gen42951" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42949" osisID="Isa.16.9" type="section"/>
entries.d21481d995d712d3841baeb0aab0e882ff2c9da4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.10" sID="gen42953" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42954" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi><hi type="italic"> Joy is taken away.</hi> He confirms, by different words, what he has now said, that the whole country shall be desolate and forsaken, so that there shall never again be in it a harvest or a vintage. When he threatens that God will cause the vine-dressers to cease to sing, he refers to an ancient custom; for when they gathered the vintage, they usually testified their joy both by dancing and by singing. Hence these words of Virgil, <hi type="italic">The exhausted vine-dresser now addresses by song his</hi> <hi type="italic">farthest rows</hi> <note n="268"> <div sID="gen42955" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42955" type="x-p"/> </note> In like manner, the sailors, when they approach the harbour, raise their shout of joy, (<foreign xml:lang="el">κἐλευσμα</foreign>,) because, having finished their toils, and escaped dangers, they see that they have hope of obtaining some leisure or refreshment. It is as if the Prophet had said, “When the produce of the harvest shall be taken away, nothing will be left to them but to lament their poverty.”<div eID="gen42954" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42953" osisID="Isa.16.10" type="section"/>
entries.f0860eb3563c42ebc33bbebe820b3bbf004c3925: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.11" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.11" sID="gen42956" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi><hi type="italic"> Therefore my bowels shall sound like a harp for Moab.</hi> Assuming the character of a Moabite, the Prophet again describes excessive lamentation, proceeding from grief so intense that even the bowels make a distressing noise; for by the sign he intended to point out the reality. We have formerly explained the object of those lively descriptions, which is, to bring the events, as it were, before our eyes, and to lead us to entertain stronger hopes of those things which appear to go beyond all belief. By again naming <hi type="italic">Kir-Hareseth</hi>, the chief city, and thus taking a part for the whole, he describes the destruction of the whole country.<div eID="gen42957" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.11" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42956" osisID="Isa.16.11" type="section"/>
entries.7a933119d5c998f3ec8b773d4a6c3df2c3406041: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.12" sID="gen42958" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42959" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">And it shall be.</hi> He again returns to that statement which he formerly noticed, namely, that idolaters in their affliction betake themselves to their idols, hoping to obtain some relief from them. Yet it means somewhat more; for while idolaters have their ordinary temples and places of worship, if any uncommon calamity befalls them, they go to another temple more sacred than the rest, expecting that there they will be more abundantly favored with the presence of their god. In like manner, the Papists of the present day, when they are reduced to any uncommon danger, (for this fault has existed in all ages,) think that they will more readily obtain their wish by running to St. Claude, or to Mary of Loretto, or to any other celebrated idol, than if they assembled in some neighboring church. They resolve that their extraordinary prayers shall be offered up in a church which is at a great distance. It is in this sense that the Prophet applies the term <hi type="italic">Sanctuary</hi> to that which was most highly celebrated among the Moabites, and says that they will go to it, but without any advantage. Now it is evident from sacred history that their most celebrated temple was dedicated to <hi type="italic">Chemosh</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Kgs.11.7">1 Kings 11:7</reference>.)<div eID="gen42959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42960" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And shall not profit by it.</hi> <note n="269"> <div sID="gen42961" type="x-p"/>{Bogus footnote}<div eID="gen42961" type="x-p"/> </note> The phrase <foreign xml:lang="he">לא יוכל</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">lo</hi> <hi type="italic">yuchal</hi>,) <hi type="italic">they shall not be able</hi>, is explained by some to mean, that they shall at length be so completely worn out that they will not have sufficient strength to go to the temple. But I think it better to render it thus, <hi type="italic">he shall not profit by it</hi>; for he shuts out the Moabites from all hope of safety, by saying that they will find no protection even in their gods.<div eID="gen42960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen42962" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">When it is seen.</hi> The word <foreign xml:lang="he">נראה</foreign>, (<hi type="italic">nirah</hi>,) <hi type="italic">seen</hi>, is emphatic. It means that idolaters are not guided by reason, but rather by the impressions made on their senses, like brute beasts: for as the beasts judge by feeling, smelling, and seeing, so idolaters have no other guide than the judgment of the flesh. Accordingly, if any one shall show that they are doing wrong, he will gain nothing by it. Though they have often known by experience that they gain nothing by so many laborious exertions, they will not desist from them, but will contrive new methods and introduce new modes of worship, hoping that God will approve of them. If they succeed according to their wish, they ascribe everything to their superstitions, and become more obstinate. If they perceive that they have derived no advantage, they reject their contrivances, condemn the superstitious worship, and curse their gods. In short, they rely altogether on the events, and do not judge of anything either by reason or by the word of God. The consequence is, that, as they are guided by what befalls them, they are continually changing their plans. But the Prophet appears to mean somewhat more, namely, that when their folly, in having hitherto labored to no purpose, shall have been openly manifested and exposed, the Moabites will come into the temple of Chemosh, rather through shame than in the exercise of judgment.<div eID="gen42962" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42958" osisID="Isa.16.12" type="section"/>
entries.3dcc397bcb5d7f776fd8a98250afdf32bda9f667: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.16.13" sID="gen42963" type="section"/> <div sID="gen42964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">This is the word.</hi> This concluding sentence is the ratification of the prophecy. It means that he has pronounced the decree of God himself, and that he has brought nothing forward that did not proceed from the Lord, and thus, laying aside the person of a man, he introduces God speaking in this manner.<div eID="gen42964" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.16.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen42963" osisID="Isa.16.13" type="section"/>
entries.dfea1126b2902e7b1e7a2f1c2ee81b662cbea347:
14. Three years. The time is fixed, not only for the sake of certainty, but likewise that believers may not become faint through longer delay. He alludes to agreements among men, in which it is customary to fix the time agreed on, which the parties are not at liberty to transgress. This is especially the case in the labors of hirelings, from whom Scripture frequently draws a comparison in this respect, that they earnestly long for the appointed day when they shall receive their reward; for they groan, as it were, under the burden, and grievously dislike their daily toils. (Job 7:1, 2, 14:6; Isaiah 21:16.) In this way the Lord says, that he fixes a day for the Moabites, in which they shall not escape from the entire destruction of their power.
With all his multitude. He expressly mentions a multitude, because their number was great, and because they boasted of it, and thought that they were invincible. When he adds, that the remnant shall be feeble, he means that there will be so great a change, that they will have no resemblance to their former condition; for nothing will be left but a sad and shocking sight.

                  <ns0:p n="10">10 And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 48. 33.</ns0:note> gladness is taken away, and joy out of the plentiful field, and in the vineyards there shall be no singing, neither shall there be shout<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing: the treaders <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">In those times they used to squeeze out the Juyce of their Grapes by treading them with their Feet, in Vessels appointed for that use, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9. 27. <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 13. 15.</ns0:note> shall tread out no wine in <ns0:hi>their</ns0:hi> presses; I have made <ns0:hi>their vintage</ns0:hi>-shouting to cease.</ns0:p>

Hereby he signifies the greatness of their approaching Ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lamity, which being so grievous to him, must needs be in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tolerable to them.</ns0:note> like an harp for Moab, and mine inward parts for Kir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />haresh.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And it shall come to pass, when it is seen that Moab is weary <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 15. 2.</ns0:note> on the high place <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">When it shall appear to them and others, that all their other Devotions are vain and ineffectual.</ns0:note>, that he shall come to his Sanctuary <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">To the Tem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of his great God <ns0:hi>Chemosh, Numb.</ns0:hi> 21. 29. 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 11. 7. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 46. from whom he shall seek and expect Succour.</ns0:note> to pray, but he shall not prevail <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">His God can neither hear nor help him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> the word that the LORD hath spoken concerning Moab <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> from then, <ns0:hi>that is,</ns0:hi> heretofore.</ns0:note> since that time <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Since the beginning of God's Revelation to me con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning <ns0:hi>Moab,</ns0:hi> and hitherto. Which Exposition seems to be confirmed by the following Words, <ns0:hi>But now.</ns0:hi>

                  <ns0:p n="14">14 But now the LORD hath spoken <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Hath made this further discovery of his Mind to me.</ns0:note>, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, Within three years <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To be computed either, 1. from the time of <ns0:hi>Ierusalems</ns0:hi> Destruction by <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar,</ns0:hi> who did, as is confessed by all, invade the <ns0:hi>Moabites</ns0:hi> at or about that time, and execute the Judgment first foretold by this Prophet, and afterwards by <ns0:hi>Ieremy, ch.</ns0:hi> 48. or rather, 2. from the time of the De<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livery of this Prophecy. Which, being uncertain, leaves us the greater Latitude for the determination of the precise time when this was fulfilled. But this is certain, from <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 1. 1. that this Prophecy must be delivered, at farthest, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore the end of <ns0:hi>Hezekiah</ns0:hi>'s Reign. And then there ariseth this great Difficulty, How this can consist with the Prophecy of <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> who above or about an hundred years after this time speaketh of <ns0:hi>Moab</ns0:hi> as a People that had <ns0:hi>been at ease from their youth,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>had not gone into captivity, Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 11. and prophesieth against them in the very same Words which <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> useth in this Prophecy? The Answer is, That they do not speak of the same time, nor of the same Cala<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mity; but <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> of a former Tribulation, and <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> of their latter Devastation. It is true, <ns0:hi>Ieremiah</ns0:hi> useth the same Words which <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> doth, and so do the later Prophets some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times use the Words of the former, to other purposes than they were first delivered, as we shall see hereafter, and as is most evident from the <ns0:hi>Revelation of St. Iohn,</ns0:hi> in which the same Words are used concerning Mystical <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> which were used by the foregoing Prophets concerning the first and literal <ns0:hi>Babylon.</ns0:hi> And although the foregoing Prophecy of <ns0:hi>Isaiah</ns0:hi> seems to speak of the same Destruction threatned by <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> and inflicted by <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar;</ns0:hi> yet this Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phecy contained in this Verse, and ushered in with ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Preface, seems to be of a differing nature, and to speak of a more speedy and less grievous Affliction that should befal them, which should be as a Pledge to assure them of the certain Accomplishment of the other Prophe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy, and of their utter Destruction. And therefore it is observable, that the Prophet doth not here say, <ns0:hi>Within three years</ns0:hi> all that I have foretold and threatned shall be fulfil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led; but onely, <ns0:hi>the glory of Moab shall be contemned, &c.</ns0:hi> which is quite another thing; and as the Terms here used are much milder, so the Judgment here denounced seems much less, than in the foregoing Prophecy. And therefore this Verse may very well be understood of some great Blow given to the <ns0:hi>Moabites,</ns0:hi> either by <ns0:hi>Sennacherib,</ns0:hi> or by his Son <ns0:hi>Esarbaddon,</ns0:hi> from which notwithstanding they in a little time recovered themselves, and flourished again, and continued so to do, till <ns0:hi>Nebuchadnezzar</ns0:hi> compleated their Destruction. And this may well enough consist with what is said of <ns0:hi>Moab's being at ease from his youth, Ier.</ns0:hi> 48. 11. which is not to be understood simply as if they had been wholly free from War and other Calamities; for the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />trary is evident both from Scripture, as 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 8. 2. 2 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 3. 24, 25. and from other Histories: but comparatively, that they had not been brought to Desolation, nor carried away into Captivity, as it is explained in the following Words, and as <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> had been at that time, and <ns0:hi>Iudah</ns0:hi> was threatned to be.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 21. 16.</ns0:note> as the years of an hireling <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Within three years precisely ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />counted; for Hirelings are very punctual in observing the Time for which they are hired; and their Thoughts and Desires run much upon it, because then they are to re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive their Wages: of which see <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 7. 1. 2. & 14. 6. And this Exposition is confirmed by comparing this Place with <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 21. 16. where the same Phrase is used of one year. So groundless is that Opinion which the Jewish Writers ga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther from this Place, compared with <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 15. 18.
